title: Process Automation, Logic, and Integration
summary: Make Salesforce do the work: triggers that scale, async jobs that recover, and integrations that don't break.

lessons.title: Order of Execution & Recursion
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, apply trigger best practices, including order of execution and recursion control, alongside declarative automation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: When you save a record, Salesforce doesn't just store it. It runs a fixed line of steps: flows, triggers, rules, then the save. This line is the **order of execution**. Knowing it tells you which automation sees which value, and why some code runs twice.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A car wash. Every car goes through the same stations in the same order: rinse, soap, brush, dry. Each station only sees what earlier stations did. Where the picture breaks: a workflow field update or a flow that updates the same record sends the car back through some stations again.

cards.title: The save line (simplified)
items: System validation (required fields, formats)
Before-save record-triggered flows
Before triggers
System validation again + custom validation rules
Duplicate rules
Save to the database (not committed yet)
After triggers
Assignment, auto-response, workflow and escalation rules
After-save record-triggered flows
Roll-up summaries + parent record updates
Commit, then post-commit work (emails, async jobs)

cards.title: Free field updates
cards.body: A **before trigger** (code that runs just before the record is saved) can change fields on `Trigger.new` for free. No DML needed: your changes are saved with the record. Changing the same record in an after trigger is not allowed on `Trigger.new`. You need another `update`, which costs a DML statement and fires the triggers again.

cards.title: Before or after trigger?
items: **Before:** set or fix fields on the same records (defaults, stamps)
**Before:** block a bad record with `addError` before it is saved
**After:** you need the record's `Id` or system fields like `CreatedDate`
**After:** create or change *other* records (child Tasks, the parent Account)
**After:** queue async work or publish events about the saved record

cards.title: Workflow re-fire
cards.body: A **workflow field update** saves the record a second time. Before update and after update triggers run **one more time**, and system validation runs again. Custom validation rules, duplicate rules and flows do not. So code that creates records in an after update trigger can create them twice. Fix: act only when a field really changed (compare with `Trigger.oldMap`).

A `static Boolean` 'already ran' flag looks safe, but it breaks bulk saves. When one DML statement holds more than 200 records, the trigger runs once per chunk of **200**, all in the SAME transaction, and static variables keep their value. Chunk 2 sees the flag already set and is skipped. No error appears, so the bug hides until a big load.

cards.title: Safer recursion guard
cards.body: `Set.add()` returns false when the Id is already there. So each record is handled once per transaction, and records in later chunks still get through. Even better: also check `Trigger.oldMap` so you only act when the field you care about really changed.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Flow, Trigger, Validate, Save.** Before-save flows first, before triggers next, then validation rules check the result. Guard recursion per record with a Set, never with one Boolean.

terms.say: The fixed list of steps Salesforce runs every time a record is saved. Like a recipe: same steps, same order, every time.
Apex that runs just before the record is saved. It can change that record's fields for free, with no extra save.
The list of records being saved right now, with their new values. In a before trigger you can change them directly.
Apex commands that change records: insert, update, delete and more. Each one counts toward a limit, and can fire triggers.
An old-style rule that changes a field after the save. It saves the record again, so update triggers run one more time.
Checks an admin sets up that block a bad save with an error message. For example: "Close Date can't be in the past."
Code that ends up starting itself again, like a trigger whose update fires the same trigger. Without a guard it loops or does work twice.
Everything that happens in one save, start to finish. It all succeeds together, or it is all undone together.
The moment the changes become final in the database. Before that, everything can still be undone.
Puts an item into a Set, a list with no repeats. It returns false if the item was already there. Handy to handle each record only once.

lessons.title: Bulk-Safe Trigger Frameworks
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, apply trigger best practices and Apex error handling for bulk-safe, maintainable logic.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Trigger code must work for 1 record or 200 at once. It also needs a clear order, so nothing surprises you. A **trigger framework** is a simple pattern: one small trigger per object hands all the work to a class. It keeps code tidy, testable and bulk-safe.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A restaurant with one host at the door. Every guest goes through the host, who seats them in order. Three hosts shouting at once would be chaos. That is why you want one trigger per object.

cards.title: Framework rules
items: **One trigger per object**, listing every event it needs
Keep the trigger thin: it hands work to a **handler class**
The handler checks `Trigger.operationType` to pick a method
No SOQL or DML inside loops: each query or save counts toward a per-transaction limit
Use Maps keyed by Id to look things up instead of querying again

cards.title: Why one trigger?
cards.body: Say one object has several triggers for the same event. Salesforce **does not guarantee their order**, and it can change between releases. Example: trigger A sets Region, trigger B reads Region. Some days B runs first and sees a blank value. One trigger plus a handler means you choose the order in code, and every developer adds logic in the same place.

cards.title: Thin trigger, fat handler
cards.body: The trigger only starts the handler. The handler picks a method for each event, in the order you choose. Each method takes the whole list, so it works for 1 record or 200, and you can unit test it.

cards.title: Block one bad record
cards.body: `addError` stops just this record (or field) from saving, and the user sees the message. Use it for rules a validation rule can't express, like checks that need a query. It works in before and after triggers, but before is faster: nothing has been saved yet.

cards.title: Custom exceptions
cards.body: A **custom exception** is your own error type. It must extend `Exception`, and its name **must end in Exception**. Why bother? Callers can catch *your* problem by name and handle it, instead of catching every error. Example: `public class PaymentException extends Exception {}`, then `throw new PaymentException('Card declined');`.

With plain DML (`insert`, `update`) or `allOrNone = true`, one `addError` fails the whole statement, and nothing saves. With `Database.insert(list, false)`, only the flagged records fail and the rest save. The catch: Salesforce rolls back the first try and runs the triggers again on the good records, so a static guard can skip them.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **One door, thin trigger, fat handler.** And never query in a loop: query once, then look things up in a Map.

terms.say: A simple pattern for triggers: one small trigger per object passes all the work to a class. Keeps code tidy, testable and safe for many records.
Works just as well for 1 record or 200 at once, without hitting limits. Like cooking for a crowd in one big pot, not 200 tiny ones.
The Apex class that holds the trigger's real logic. The trigger just calls it. Here you test the code and choose the order of steps.
Tells the code which event is running, like BEFORE_INSERT or AFTER_UPDATE. The handler uses it to pick the right method.
Salesforce's language for asking the database for records. Each query counts toward a limit, so never run one inside a loop.
Apex commands that save changes: insert, update, delete. Each one counts toward a limit, so do it once for the whole list.
A lookup table: each key points to one value. With Ids as keys, you find a record instantly instead of searching or querying again.
Marks one record, or one of its fields, as bad so it won't save. The user sees your message. Like a teacher returning one test with a note.
Your own error type. It must extend Exception, and its name must end in Exception, like PaymentException.
A setting on a DML save. When true (the default), one bad record fails the whole save. When false, the good records still save.

lessons.title: Future vs Queueable
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, implement asynchronous Apex using future methods and Queueable Apex, including chaining.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Some work is too slow, or not allowed, during a save. Calling another system from a trigger is one example. **Asynchronous Apex** (code that runs a bit later, in its own transaction) moves that work out. The user doesn't wait, and the job gets its own, often higher, limits. `@future` and Queueable are the two simplest ways.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A **future method** is a letter in a postbox: it goes, but you get no tracking number. A **Queueable** is a tracked parcel: you get a job Id, can pack bigger things, and can send the next parcel when it lands. Neither one promises an exact start time.

cards.title: `@future`
cards.body: A future method is `static` and `void`. It takes **only primitives or collections of primitives** (like `Set<Id>`), never sObjects. Why? The record could change before the job runs, so you pass Ids and re-query fresh data inside. Add `callout=true` when it calls another system.

cards.title: Queueable
cards.body: A Queueable can hold **sObjects and complex types** in member variables. They are saved with the job and restored when it runs, except `transient` ones, which come back null. `System.enqueueJob` returns a **job Id** you can look up in `AsyncApexJob` to see its status.

cards.title: Future or Queueable?
items: **Need a job Id to track it?** Queueable
**Need to pass records or objects?** Queueable
**Need step 2 to start after step 1?** Queueable (chain it)
**Just a tiny fire-and-forget call with Ids?** `@future` still works
Salesforce now **recommends Queueable** for new code: same uses, more control

cards.title: Limits to memorize
items: **50** future calls per transaction
**50** `enqueueJob` calls in a synchronous transaction
Only **1** child job from an executing Queueable (or any async transaction)
Chain depth: no limit, except **5** in Developer Edition and trial orgs

cards.title: Delay and control
cards.body: `System.enqueueJob(job, delayMinutes)` waits **0-10 minutes** before the job can start, for example to let another system catch up. `AsyncOptions` gives more control: `MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes`, `MaximumQueueableStackDepth` (to cap a chain), and a `DuplicateSignature` that blocks the same job being queued twice. Apex tests ignore the delay.

You **can't call a future method from a future or batch** context. It throws an error at run time. This bites when a trigger calls `@future` and a batch job later updates the same records. Check `System.isFuture()` and `System.isBatch()` first, or use a Queueable instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Future = Fire and Forget. Queueable = Queue it, Track it, Chain it.** Pass Ids to a future; pass anything to a Queueable. From async code, only one child job.

terms.say: Code that runs a bit later, in its own transaction with its own limits. The user doesn't wait for it to finish.
A static, void method marked @future that runs later. You get no job Id. It only accepts simple values, like Ids, not whole records.
A class you put in a line to run later. You get a job Id, it can hold whole records, and it can start one next job.
Simple values: numbers, text, dates, true/false and Ids. Not whole records. So pass Ids and look the records up again.
Salesforce records inside Apex, like an Account or a record of your own custom object.
The call that puts a Queueable in line to run. It hands back a job Id so you can track the job.
The ID of an async job. Use it to check how the job is doing: queued, running, done or failed.
How many jobs in a row can each start the next one. No limit in normal orgs, but only 5 jobs (counting the first one) in Developer Edition and trial orgs.
Extra settings when you queue a job: a minimum delay, a max chain depth, and a signature that stops the same job being queued twice.
Returns true if the code is already running inside a future method. Check it first, because a future can't call another future.

lessons.title: Transaction Finalizers
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, implement asynchronous Apex with error recovery using Transaction Finalizers.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sometimes a Queueable crashes. It hits an **uncaught exception** or a governor limit. Its DML rolls back, and try/catch can't catch limit errors. A **Transaction Finalizer** is a class that runs after the Queueable ends, success or failure. It lets you log the problem or retry.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: The cleanup crew after a party. It shows up when the party ends, even if the party crashed. It writes down what happened and can book one new party. Where it stops working: the crew can't save the party's work. The Queueable's DML is already rolled back.

cards.title: Attach a finalizer
cards.body: Implement `Finalizer`, then call `System.attachFinalizer()` inside `execute()` (not in the constructor, which runs before the job is queued). The finalizer runs after the Queueable finishes, success OR failure, so one class handles both outcomes by checking `getResult()`.

cards.title: `FinalizerContext` gives you
items: `getResult()`: `SUCCESS` or `UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`
`getException()`: the error that ended the job (null when it succeeded)
`getAsyncApexJobId()`: the job Id (matches `AsyncApexJob`)
`getRequestId()`: the request Id, for Event Monitoring logs

cards.title: Rules
items: **One** finalizer per Queueable
Runs in its **own transaction** with fresh limits (mostly the synchronous ones, like 100 SOQL queries)
Its DML commits even when the Queueable's DML rolled back
Can enqueue **one** async job and make callouts
A failing Queueable can be re-enqueued **5** consecutive times, then it stops

cards.title: When to reach for it
items: **try/catch** handles errors you expect, but can't catch a governor limit
**A finalizer** runs even after a limit error: log it, alert someone, or retry
**Polling `AsyncApexJob`** later also finds failures, but it's slow and needs a scheduled job
For **Batch Apex**, the matching tool is the `BatchApexErrorEvent` platform event, not a finalizer

cards.title: What the finalizer remembers
cards.body: The finalizer uses its variables **as they are when the Queueable ends**. So changes made after attaching it still count. But `transient` variables (ones skipped when the object is saved) arrive as null.

A `static` retry counter doesn't work. Statics reset in every new transaction, and the finalizer runs in its own, so it always sees 0. The job retries until the platform's 5-retry cap, not your limit. Pass the attempt count through the Queueable's constructor instead: `new SyncJob(ids, attempt + 1)`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Finalizer = the cleanup crew.** One crew per job, its own transaction, one new job, five retries max.

terms.say: An error that no try/catch catches. The job stops right there and its changes are undone.
A per-transaction cap Salesforce sets, like 100 queries. Hit one and the job stops at once. Even try/catch can't catch it.
All the job's database changes are undone, as if they never happened. Like pressing undo on everything at once.
A class that runs after a Queueable ends, whether it worked or crashed. Use it to log the problem or try again.
Hooks your finalizer onto the running Queueable. Call it inside execute(). Only one finalizer per job.
Hands the finalizer the error that ended the job. Use it to log what went wrong.
The result when the Queueable crashed with an error nothing caught. The other possible result is SUCCESS.
The record Salesforce keeps for each async job, with its status and errors. You can query it to check on a job.
Marks a variable to skip when the object is saved. So the finalizer gets it back as null.
A static variable is shared by all code in one transaction. It starts fresh in every new transaction, so it can't carry a count to the finalizer.

lessons.title: Batch Apex & Scheduling
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, implement Batch Apex and Schedulable Apex for large data volumes.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Some jobs touch millions of records. No single transaction can do that: limits cap queries, rows and CPU time. **Batch Apex** splits the records into chunks and runs each chunk as its own transaction. **Schedulable Apex** starts code at a set time, like every night at 2 AM. Use Batch for big data; use a Queueable for smaller jobs.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A dishwasher run one rack at a time. Each rack (chunk) gets fresh water (fresh governor limits). Schedulable is the timer that starts the machine at night. Where it stops working: racks share nothing unless you add `Database.Stateful`.

cards.title: Batch skeleton
cards.body: `start()` finds the records once, `execute()` runs once per chunk, and `finish()` runs once at the end (send a summary, start the next job). Each `execute()` gets **fresh governor limits**, so one bad chunk fails alone and the others still save. Start it with `Database.executeBatch(new CleanupBatch(), 200)`.

cards.title: `QueryLocator` vs `Iterable`
items: `QueryLocator`: up to **50 million** records
`QueryLocator` scope: max **2,000** (default 200); a bigger number is cut to 2,000
`Iterable`: the normal SOQL row limit (**50,000**) applies
`Iterable`: for custom logic or non-SOQL sources; no upper limit on scope

cards.title: `Database.Stateful`
cards.body: `Database.Stateful` keeps **instance variables** (like counters and error lists) from one chunk to the next. Without it, each chunk starts with a fresh copy, so a total in `finish()` is 0. The cost: the job's state is saved after every chunk, which makes it slower, so use it only when you need it. `Static` variables never carry over, even with it.

cards.title: Queue, chain, recover
items: **5** batch jobs queued or active at once
Up to **100** more wait in the **Apex flex queue** (status Holding)
Chain batches by calling `Database.executeBatch` in `finish()`, so B starts only after A is done
Add `Database.RaisesPlatformEvents`: a crashed chunk publishes a `BatchApexErrorEvent` with the failed record Ids

cards.title: Schedule it
cards.body: The cron string reads seconds, minutes, hours, day of month, month, day of week. `?` means 'any' and goes in one of the two day fields. An org can have at most **100** scheduled Apex jobs. To run a batch just once later, `System.scheduleBatch(job, 'name', 60)` needs no Schedulable class.

Scheduled Apex **can't make synchronous callouts**, and `callout=true` doesn't exist for it. From its `execute()`, start a Queueable or Batch that implements `Database.AllowsCallouts`, or a `@future(callout=true)` method. Inside a batch, make callouts before any DML in the same `execute()`, or you get 'uncommitted work pending'.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Start, Execute, Finish: find, chew, tidy up.** Cron starts with **S M H**: Seconds, Minutes, Hours.

terms.say: Apex that splits a huge set of records into chunks. Each chunk runs as its own transaction, so millions of records can be handled.
Apex that starts at a set time, like every night at 2 AM. Like an alarm clock for your code.
Caps Salesforce sets per transaction, like how many queries or saves you may do. Each batch chunk gets a fresh set.
What start() returns when it uses one SOQL query. It can feed up to 50 million records to the batch.
What start() can return for custom logic or data that isn't a query. The normal 50,000-row query limit still applies.
How many records each execute() chunk gets. Default 200. With a QueryLocator the max is 2,000.
Lets a batch remember its instance variables, like a running count, from one chunk to the next. Static variables still reset.
A waiting room for batch jobs. Up to 100 wait there, marked Holding, until one of the 5 active slots frees up.
A short text that says when to run, read as seconds, minutes, hours, day, month, weekday. "0 0 2 * * ?" means every night at 2 AM.
Add this to a batch class so it may call other systems over the internet.

lessons.title: Pick the Right Async Tool
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, choose the appropriate asynchronous Apex tool.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Salesforce gives you several ways to run code later, and the exam loves asking which to pick. Why it matters: the wrong tool hits a limit (too many rows, too many jobs) or can't do the job at all (no callouts, no records as input). Look for the clues: how much data, what inputs, a set time, or many listeners.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Ways to send things. A postcard is quick and simple (future). A tracked parcel can hand off to the next stop (Queueable). A moving truck carries huge loads (Batch). An alarm clock starts things on time (Schedulable). A radio show reaches anyone tuned in (Platform Events).

cards.title: Decision cheat sheet
items: Simple callout from a trigger: `@future(callout=true)` or Queueable
sObject inputs, a job Id, chaining: **Queueable**
Wait a few minutes first: **Queueable with a delay** (0-10 min)
Guaranteed cleanup on failure: **Queueable + Finalizer**
Millions of records: **Batch Apex**
Run at a set time: **Schedulable**
Many listeners the sender should not know about: **Platform Events**

cards.title: Triggers + callouts
cards.body: A trigger **can't make a synchronous callout** (a call to another system that waits for the answer). The record is still in the middle of saving, holding database locks, and the user would wait on a slow server. Hand the work to async Apex that allows callouts, and pass record Ids. Example: after insert on Order, enqueue `new OrderSyncJob(orderIds)`.

cards.title: Key limits side by side
items: **Future:** 50 calls per transaction; primitives only; none from batch or future code
**Queueable:** 50 jobs from synchronous code, only 1 from async code
**Batch:** 5 active jobs, 100 more in the flex queue; up to 50 million records with a `QueryLocator`
**Scheduled:** at most 100 scheduled Apex jobs in the org
**Callouts:** 100 per transaction, in sync and async code alike

cards.title: Monitoring
cards.body: Batch, Queueable and future jobs all show up in `AsyncApexJob` and on the Apex Jobs page, with status and error counts. `System.enqueueJob` and `Database.executeBatch` return the job Id, so you can query that one job. A future method returns nothing, so you have to search for it. `System.schedule` returns a `CronTrigger` Id.

Calling `Database.executeBatch` from a trigger on every save floods the limit of **5** active batch jobs and the 100-slot flex queue. A busy day of edits soon fails with an error. Batch is for **big bulk work**, not quick per-record reactions. For those, enqueue one Queueable per transaction with all the record Ids.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **F-Q-B-S**: Future (fast and simple), Queueable (flexible), Batch (big), Schedule (clock). Add **PE** when many listeners must react.

terms.say: Apex calling another system over the internet, like a shipping service, and getting its answer back.
A call to another system where the code stops and waits for the answer. A trigger can't do it, because the record is still mid-save.
Async Apex that can take whole records, gives you a job Id, and can start one next job. The flexible all-rounder.
A class that runs after a Queueable ends, even if it crashed. Good for cleanup, logging or one retry.
Async Apex for huge jobs. It splits millions of records into chunks, each with its own fresh limits.
Apex that starts at a set time, like every night at 2 AM. The alarm clock of async tools.
Messages sent out for anyone listening. The sender doesn't know or care who reacts. Like a radio show.
The record Salesforce keeps for each async job, with its status and errors. You can look it up or see it on the Apex Jobs page.
The call that starts a Batch Apex job. Only 5 batch jobs can run at once, so don't call it on every save.
A waiting line for extra batch jobs, up to 100. They wait there until one of the 5 active batch slots frees up.

lessons.title: Platform Events
lessons.objective: Identify the appropriate publish/subscribe logic for platform events.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **platform event** is a message one part of your system sends out for others to hear. The sender doesn't know who is listening. Listeners can be Apex, flows, LWC or outside systems. Why it matters: when a team adds a new reaction, they add a listener, and the sender's code doesn't change. The pieces stay loosely tied together.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A school loudspeaker announcement. The office speaks once, and every class that cares reacts. Nobody phones each room. Where it stops working: you can't edit or look up an announcement later. Events can't be updated or queried like records.

cards.title: Publish
cards.body: Event objects end in `__e`. `EventBus.publish` returns a `SaveResult`. For **Publish After Commit** events, each call counts as one DML statement (150 per transaction). Publish Immediately calls have their own limit of 150. So build a list and publish it in one call, not one call per record.

cards.title: Publish behavior
items: **Publish After Commit**: sent only if the transaction commits
**Publish Immediately**: sent right away, even if the transaction **rolls back**
Use Immediately for error logs that must survive a rollback
A successful `SaveResult` only means the publish was **queued**

cards.title: Subscribers
items: Apex trigger (`after insert` only)
Platform event-triggered flow
LWC via `lightning/empApi`
External: **Pub/Sub API** or CometD

cards.title: Event triggers are different
cards.body: By default they run as the **Automated Process** user, so new records show it as creator. Change that with `PlatformEventSubscriberConfig`. They get batches of up to **2,000** events, in a separate transaction from the publisher, and use the synchronous limits. Like other triggers, they generally can't make callouts: enqueue a Queueable for that.

cards.title: Resume after failure
cards.body: `setResumeCheckpoint` saves your place. If the trigger dies, the next run starts after that event. Or throw `EventBus.RetryableException` to resend the whole batch (up to 9 times).

Events published **immediately** are **not** undone by `Database.rollback` or a failed transaction. And you can't query or update events like records: there is no SOQL on `__e` objects. To catch up on missed events, a subscriber replays them from a saved Replay ID. High-volume events are kept for 72 hours.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **After Commit waits for the bell. Immediately shouts now.** Event triggers: `after insert` only.

terms.say: A message one part of your system sends out for others to hear. The sender doesn't know who is listening.
The Apex call that sends out platform events. Each call counts toward a limit of 150 per transaction, and gives back a SaveResult. Publish a whole list in one call.
The receipt you get after publishing. Success only means the event was queued to send, not that anyone got it yet.
The event goes out only if the whole transaction saves for good. If the transaction is undone, the event is never sent.
The event goes out right away, even if the transaction is undone later. Good for error logs that must survive.
Salesforce's API that outside systems use to listen for events or send them. CometD is an older way to listen.
A built-in system user. Platform event triggers run as this user by default, not as the person who published.
Setup for a platform event trigger: which user it runs as and how many events it gets per batch.
Saves your place in the batch of events. If the trigger fails, the next run starts after that event, not from the top.
Throw it to have the whole batch of events sent to your trigger again, a bit later. Up to 9 retries.

lessons.title: Change Data Capture
lessons.objective: Identify the appropriate publish/subscribe logic for Change Data Capture events.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Change Data Capture (CDC)** tells other systems when records change. Salesforce sends a change event each time a record is created, updated, deleted or undeleted. You just **select the objects** in Setup. No publishing code. Why it matters: a data warehouse or ERP can stay in sync in near real time, without polling Salesforce for changes every hour.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A diary Salesforce keeps for you. Every change to a chosen object gets an entry, and other systems read it to stay in sync. Where it stops working: only committed changes get written. Rolled-back changes leave no entry.

cards.title: Names & channels
items: Standard: `AccountChangeEvent`
Custom: `Invoice__ChangeEvent` (`__c` becomes `__ChangeEvent`)
Channel: `/data/AccountChangeEvent`
All selected objects: `/data/ChangeEvents`

cards.title: Read the header
cards.body: The `ChangeEventHeader` says what happened: `changeType` (CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE, UNDELETE), `recordIds`, `changedFields`, `commitUser`, `entityName`. `changeOrigin` names the API client that made the change, so a sync can skip its own write-backs and avoid an endless loop.

cards.title: Commit-only
cards.body: Change events go out only **after the transaction commits**. Rolled-back changes make no events, and there is no Publish Immediately option. Events are kept for **3 days**, so a subscriber that was down can replay what it missed. Note: formula fields are never included in change events.

cards.title: What's in an update event
cards.body: In Apex, fields that **didn't change are null**. Check `changedFields`, and `nulledFields` for fields set to null on purpose. One event can cover **many records**, so loop over `recordIds`.

A change event trigger has **no Trigger.old**. It's an after insert trigger on the event, not on the record, and it runs later, in its own transaction, as the Automated Process user. To see what changed, read `changedFields` in the header. Never send null fields on to another system as if they were real values.

cards.title: CDC or platform event?
items: **CDC:** Salesforce publishes for you, whenever selected records change
**CDC:** fixed shape: the record's fields plus a header
**Platform event:** you design the fields and publish it yourself
**Platform event:** for business moments that aren't just a record change, like 'payment failed'
**Platform event:** can publish immediately; CDC only after commit

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **PE = you write the message. CDC = Salesforce writes the diary of record changes.**

terms.say: Salesforce sends a message whenever a chosen object's records are created, updated, deleted or undeleted. You pick objects in Setup, no code to publish.
The message Salesforce sends when a record is created, updated, deleted or undeleted. Other systems read it to stay in sync.
The address listeners tune in to, like a radio station. One per object, or /data/ChangeEvents for all selected objects.
The part of a change event that says what happened: which kind of change, which records, which fields, and who made it.
The list of fields that changed in an update. Read it, because fields that didn't change arrive as null.
The Ids of the records this event is about. One event can cover many records, so loop over them all.
The user whose save made the change. Handy to know who did it.
Asking again for events that were already sent, like rewinding a recording. Change events are kept for 3 days.
Lists fields someone emptied on purpose. It tells a real "made blank" apart from "didn't change", since both show null.
In normal update triggers, the records as they were before the change. Change event triggers don't have it.

lessons.title: Outbound Callouts
lessons.objective: Apply programmatic integration techniques for outbound communication, including callouts, Named Credentials and Continuations.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **callout** is your Apex calling another system over the internet, like a tax or shipping service. You send a request and wait for the answer. While Apex waits, the user often waits too. That's why Salesforce limits how many calls you make and how long you wait, and why slow calls belong in async Apex.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Phoning a shop from your desk. A **Named Credential** is the saved contact: number plus login, so the password never sits on a sticky note. Where it stops working: you can't phone while unsaved work sits on your desk (pending DML).

cards.title: REST callout
cards.body: The `callout:` prefix uses a Named Credential, so no Remote Site Setting is needed and no password sits in code. `send()` returns a response for any HTTP status, even 500 or 503. Check `res.getStatusCode()` before you read the body.

cards.title: Callout limits
items: **100** callouts per transaction
Default timeout **10 s**, max **120 s** per callout
Max **120 s** total callout time per transaction
Body size: **6 MB** sync, **12 MB** async

cards.title: Named + External Credentials
cards.body: A **Named Credential** holds the URL. An **External Credential** holds the login method (OAuth, JWT, custom headers) and its principals. Why split them? Secrets stay out of code, and one login setup can serve several endpoints. A named principal is one shared login; a per-user principal lets each user sign in as themselves. Users get a principal through a **permission set**.

DML **then** a callout in one transaction throws **CalloutException: You have uncommitted work pending**. Salesforce can't hold your unsaved changes while it waits on another server. Queuing async Apex (future, Queueable, batch), scheduling Apex or sending email count as pending work too. Call out first, or move the callout to async. Queries and debug lines are fine.

cards.title: SOAP and test mocks
cards.body: For SOAP, import the WSDL with **WSDL2Apex** (Generate from WSDL) to get typed classes instead of building XML by hand. Tests can't make real callouts, so you fake the reply. Test SOAP with `WebServiceMock`; test REST with `HttpCalloutMock` through `Test.setMock`. If the test inserts data first, put the callout between `Test.startTest()` and `Test.stopTest()`.

cards.title: Continuation
cards.body: A **Continuation** runs a long callout from LWC, Aura or Visualforce without tying up a server thread. Why: every org has a limit on requests running longer than 5 seconds, and slow callouts eat it up. The method returns the Continuation; a callback method gets the response. Use `@AuraEnabled(continuation=true cacheable=true)`. Up to **3** parallel callouts per Continuation, timeout up to **120 s**.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Call first, save second.** And an HTTP 503 doesn't throw: check `getStatusCode()` before you parse the body.

terms.say: Your Apex calling another system over the internet, like a tax service. You send a request and wait for the answer.
A saved setting with the address of another system, linked to how to log in. Your code never holds the password.
Holds how to log in to the other system, like OAuth or a token in a header. A Named Credential points to it.
The login identity an External Credential uses: one shared login, or each user's own. Users get it through a permission set.
An older allow-list of web addresses Apex may call. Not needed when you call through a Named Credential.
The error a callout throws when it can't go ahead or fails, like calling out while unsaved changes are waiting.
Reads a SOAP service's WSDL, its contract file, and writes ready-made Apex classes to call that service.
A fake SOAP service for tests. Tests can't make real callouts, so it hands back a pretend answer.
A fake REST service for tests. Set it with Test.setMock, and your callout gets a pretend response instead of a real one.
Lets a page built with LWC, Aura or Visualforce wait for a slow callout without tying up a Salesforce server. Up to 3 callouts each.

lessons.title: Inbound: Apex REST & SOAP
lessons.objective: Apply programmatic integration techniques for inbound communication using Apex REST and Apex SOAP web services.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sometimes outside systems need to call **into** Salesforce and run your logic. You can turn an Apex class into a web service. **Apex REST** uses URLs and JSON. **Apex SOAP** uses a WSDL contract and XML. When? The standard APIs already create and read records. Build your own only for custom logic, like creating an order and its lines in one transaction.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A drive-through window. The menu board (`urlMapping` or WSDL) says what you can order. The window must face the street (`global`), and it's always open, no setup needed (`static`). You decide what to hand back, including the status code.

cards.title: Apex REST
cards.body: This class answers GET calls at `/services/apexrest/orders/{id}`. The caller must be signed in (OAuth token or session Id). Apex runs in system mode, so add `with sharing` and use `WITH USER_MODE` queries to respect the caller's access.

cards.title: Apex REST rules
items: Class is `global`; methods are `global static`
Annotations: `@HttpGet`, `@HttpPost`, `@HttpPut`, `@HttpPatch`, `@HttpDelete`
Only **one method per annotation** in a class
`@HttpGet` and `@HttpDelete` take **no parameters** (no body); read `RestContext.request.params`
JSON keys must match parameter names; order doesn't matter
Read and write with `RestContext.request` and `RestContext.response`

cards.body: If an `@HttpPost` method **has parameters**, the JSON body fills them and **requestBody stays empty**. Need the raw body, for logging or a custom format? Use **no parameters** and read `RestContext.request.requestBody` (a Blob, so call `toString()`). Then parse it with `JSON.deserialize`.

cards.title: Status codes you get for free
items: **200**: success with a return value
**204**: a successful `void` PATCH
**400**: an unhandled custom (user) exception
**404**: no `urlMapping` matches the URL
**500**: an unhandled system exception, like a null pointer
Anything else, like **201** or **422**: set `RestContext.response.statusCode` yourself
Fields that are null are left out of the returned JSON

cards.title: Apex SOAP
cards.body: Use `webservice static` in a `global` class. Generate the WSDL from the class page and give it to the caller.

cards.title: SOAP rules
cards.body: `webservice` methods can't be overloaded (two methods with one name). They can't take or return a **Map** or Set. To send a custom type, use an inner class with `webservice` member variables. The caller needs the WSDL generated from your class, plus a session Id or OAuth token on every call.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **G.S. = Global Static.** Every inbound Apex web method needs both.

terms.say: Turns an Apex class into a web address outside systems can call, using URLs and JSON.
Turns Apex methods into a SOAP web service. Callers follow a WSDL contract and send XML.
A contract file that lists a SOAP service's methods and data types. You give it to the caller so they know what to send.
The path your Apex REST class answers at, after /services/apexrest/. Like the menu board: it says what can be ordered here.
The widest access level. Code and callers outside your app or package can reach it. Inbound web service classes must be global.
Belongs to the class itself, not to one object made from it. So it can run without creating an object first.
Marks the method that answers POST calls, usually to create something. A class may have only one.
Gives your REST method the incoming request and the response you send back, including its status code.
The raw body of the incoming request. It stays empty when your method has parameters, because Salesforce already used it to fill them.
The keyword that makes an Apex method callable over SOAP. It goes with static, inside a global class.

lessons.title: Flow Meets Apex
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, choose between declarative automation and Apex, and expose Apex to Flow with invocable actions.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Admins build lots of automation in **Flow**, a point-and-click tool. Sometimes Flow needs something it can't do alone, like complex math or a callout. An **invocable method** is Apex that Flow can call like any other action. Why it matters: admins keep owning the process; developers write only the hard part. The exam asks when to pick Flow and when to pick code.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Flow is a LEGO set, and Apex is a custom-made brick. An invocable method is a brick shaped to snap into the set. Where it stops working: Flow hands your brick a whole bag of requests at once, not one at a time.

cards.title: Invocable action
cards.body: Flow can now call **Score Leads**; the `label` is the name admins see, and `category` groups it in Flow Builder. The inner class bundles several inputs with `@InvocableVariable` (fields must be `public` or `global`). Set `callout=true` when the action calls another system.

cards.title: `@InvocableMethod` rules
items: **One** per class; the class must be an outer class
`static`, and `public` or `global`
**One** parameter: a List (or List of Lists) of primitives, sObjects or an `@InvocableVariable` class
Returns a List or `void`
No other annotation alongside it except `@Deprecated`, so it can't also be `@AuraEnabled`

cards.body: Flow **batches interviews**. 200 records can reach your method as **one call with a 200-item list**. SOQL in a loop over that list hits the limit. Return outputs in the **same size and order** as the inputs: output 5 goes to interview 5. An uncaught exception fails every interview in the batch, so catch errors per input.

cards.title: One result per input, in order
cards.body: One query for the whole batch. Looping over the inputs (not the query rows) keeps every output lined up with its interview, even when a record has no score.

cards.title: Flow or trigger?
items: Simple updates to the same record: **before-save flow**
Logic admins will maintain: **Flow**
Complex logic, heavy data, bulk callouts: **Apex**
Undelete (flows can't start on it), or a roll-up over a lookup: **Apex trigger**
Reusable Apex inside Flow: **invocable action**

cards.title: Apex types and callouts in Flow
cards.body: Flow can hold an **Apex-defined** variable: a class whose fields use `@AuraEnabled`. Flow reads and sets each field, so one variable can carry a whole structured result, like a weather report. Need a callout from a record-triggered flow? Put the action on the **Run Asynchronously** path, which runs after the record is committed.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **One door, one list in, one list out.** That's an invocable method.

terms.say: Salesforce's point-and-click tool for automation. Admins build it from boxes and arrows, with no code.
Apex that Flow can call like any other action. It takes one list in and hands one list back.
Marks a field in a class so Flow sees it as an input or output. Lets you pass several values together.
A class written inside another class. Here it bundles several Flow inputs into one object.
A top-level class, not written inside another class. An invocable method must live in one.
One run of a flow is one interview. Many runs get bundled, so your method gets one call with a big list.
A record-triggered flow that runs before the record is saved. The fastest way to update fields on that same record.
A flow that starts by itself when a record is created, updated or deleted.
A Flow variable whose type is your own Apex class. Flow can read and set each of its fields marked @AuraEnabled.
A separate path in a record-triggered flow that runs a bit later, after the save. Callouts are allowed there.

lessons.title: Database Methods & Safe SOQL
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, use Database class methods, handle mixed DML, and write secure dynamic SOQL.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Plain `insert` or `update` is all-or-nothing: one bad row and every row rolls back. The `Database` class gives you more control. You can save the good rows and report the bad ones, undo part of your work, and build queries at run time. Why care? Imports and integrations rarely have perfect data. The risk: careless run-time queries can let users inject their own SOQL.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A teacher grading a stack of tests. Plain DML throws out the whole stack if one test is wrong. `Database.insert(list, false)` grades each test alone and returns notes on the bad ones. Where it stops working: the teacher keeps no notes for you unless you read the results, and a failed test never gets a record Id.

cards.title: Partial success
cards.body: `allOrNone = false`: good rows save, and bad rows report errors. Results come back in the same order as your list, so result `i` belongs to row `i`. A failed row has no Id (`getId()` is null), so log something from `rows[i]`, like its external key, to find it later.

cards.title: Upsert by external Id
cards.body: Upsert matches on the **external Id field**, so you need no Salesforce Ids. A match updates the record; no match inserts a new one, and `isCreated()` tells you which. If two records share that external Id, that row fails with an error. Typical use: a nightly sync where the ERP sends its own customer numbers.

cards.title: Mixed DML
cards.body: DML on **setup objects** (`User`, `Group`, `GroupMember`, `PermissionSetAssignment`, `UserRole`) plus normal objects in one transaction throws `MIXED_DML_OPERATION`. Why? Changing users and access recalculates sharing, which can't mix with normal record saves. Changing the order doesn't help. Move one side to `@future` or Queueable, passing Ids. In tests, wrap the setup DML in `System.runAs`.

cards.title: Safe dynamic SOQL
cards.body: Pass values through a bind Map, so input stays data, never query text. `Database.query` binds only simple variables (`:acctId`, not `:acct.Id`). Field and object names **can't be bound**, so check them against Schema describe results (does the field exist, `isAccessible()`) before adding them to the string. `USER_MODE` also enforces the user's access.

Gluing user input into the string for `Database.query` invites **SOQL injection**. Example: input `x' OR Name != '` turns a filter into 'return everything'. Use bind variables, `Database.queryWithBinds` or `String.escapeSingleQuotes`. `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` does not stop it: it checks field access, not what the query means.

cards.title: Undo button
cards.body: `Database.setSavepoint()` marks a spot, and `Database.rollback(sp)` undoes the DML since then. Each one counts as a DML statement. A rollback doesn't reset static variables or clear Ids on your sObjects, so clone a record before inserting it again. Rolling back to an earlier savepoint voids later ones. Before a callout, call `Database.releaseSavepoint(sp)`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **False means forgiving:** `Database.insert(list, false)` keeps the good and reports the bad. Bind your values; never glue them in.

terms.say: A save setting. False means the good rows save and the bad ones just report errors. True, the default, fails the whole list.
Insert or update in one step. If a matching record exists, it is updated. If not, a new one is made.
A field holding another system's own ID for the record. Upsert can match on it, so you need no Salesforce Ids.
Records that control users and access, like User, Group and UserRole. Saving them with normal records at once causes an error.
The error from saving setup objects and normal records in one transaction. Fix it by moving one side to async Apex.
In tests, runs code as a chosen user. It also lets a test save setup and normal records without the mixed DML error.
When user input is glued into a query and changes what the query does. Like someone slipping an extra line into your shopping list.
Placeholders in a query, like :name, filled with a value safely. The value is only data, never part of the query itself.
Puts a backslash before every single quote in user input. Then the input can't close your text early and add its own query parts.
A marked spot in a transaction. Rolling back to it undoes every database change since then. Setting and rolling back each count toward the save-command limit.

flashcards.front: Which runs first: a before-save flow or a before trigger?
flashcards.back: The flow goes first. Order: before-save record-triggered flows, then before triggers, then custom validation rules.

flashcards.front: What runs again after a workflow field update?
flashcards.back: The record saves a second time, so before update and after update triggers run one more time. Custom validation rules do not run again.

flashcards.front: How many records does a trigger get at a time?
flashcards.back: Up to 200 per chunk. One DML statement with more records runs the trigger once per 200-record chunk, all in the same transaction, so static variables carry over between chunks.

flashcards.front: What is the best way to stop trigger recursion?
flashcards.back: Remember each record you handled in a `static Set<Id>`. A `static Boolean` wrongly skips the later 200-record chunks.

flashcards.front: Why keep only one trigger per object?
flashcards.back: Salesforce does not guarantee the order of several triggers on the same object and event. One trigger plus a handler class lets you control the order.

flashcards.front: What does `addError()` do?
flashcards.back: It stops that record (or field) from saving and shows the message. With Database methods and `allOrNone = false`, the other records still save.

flashcards.front: How must you name a custom exception?
flashcards.back: It must extend `Exception`, and the class name must end in 'Exception', like `PaymentException`.

flashcards.front: What can you pass into an `@future` method?
flashcards.back: Only primitives or collections of primitives. No sObjects: pass Ids and re-query inside the method.

flashcards.front: How many `@future` calls can one transaction make?
flashcards.back: 50 per transaction (synchronous code or a Queueable). From batch or future code: none at all, so use a Queueable there.

flashcards.front: How many Queueable jobs can you enqueue in one transaction?
flashcards.back: 50 with `System.enqueueJob` from a synchronous transaction. Only 1 child job from an executing Queueable.

flashcards.front: How deep can a Queueable chain go?
flashcards.back: No limit, except 5 (parent included) in Developer Edition and trial orgs. You can set your own cap with `AsyncOptions.MaximumQueueableStackDepth`.

flashcards.front: How do you make a Queueable wait before it starts?
flashcards.back: Call `System.enqueueJob(job, minutes)` with 0-10 minutes, or set `AsyncOptions.MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes`.

flashcards.front: How do you stop the same Queueable being queued twice?
flashcards.back: Set `AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature`, built with `QueueableDuplicateSignature.Builder`. A matching second enqueue throws a `DuplicateMessageException`.

flashcards.front: How do you let a Queueable make callouts?
flashcards.back: Make the class implement `Database.AllowsCallouts`. Without it, a callout inside `execute()` fails.

flashcards.front: How do you write and attach a Transaction Finalizer?
flashcards.back: Implement `Finalizer` with `void execute(FinalizerContext ctx)`. Attach it with `System.attachFinalizer()` inside `Queueable.execute()`.

flashcards.front: What can `ctx.getResult()` return in a finalizer?
flashcards.back: A `ParentJobResult`: `SUCCESS` or `UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`. On `UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`, `ctx.getException()` returns the error; on success it returns null.

flashcards.front: How many times can a finalizer re-enqueue a failing Queueable?
flashcards.back: Up to 5 consecutive times. Then the platform stops it.

flashcards.front: Which three methods does a Batch Apex class have?
flashcards.back: `start()`, `execute(scope)` and `finish()`. Each one takes a `Database.BatchableContext`.

flashcards.front: How many records can a batch `QueryLocator` return?
flashcards.back: Up to 50 million. The scope can be at most 2,000 (default 200).

flashcards.front: What limit applies when batch `start()` returns an `Iterable`?
flashcards.back: The normal SOQL row limit of 50,000. There is no upper limit on scope size.

flashcards.front: What does `Database.Stateful` do?
flashcards.back: It keeps instance variables from one `execute()` chunk to the next. Static variables still reset.

flashcards.front: How many batch jobs can run at the same time?
flashcards.back: 5 queued or active. Up to 100 more wait in the Apex flex queue with Holding status.

flashcards.front: In what order are Apex cron fields written?
flashcards.back: Seconds Minutes Hours Day_of_month Month Day_of_week [Year]. Example: `'0 0 2 * * ?'` means 2:00 AM every day.

flashcards.front: Can scheduled Apex make a callout?
flashcards.back: Not a synchronous one. Start a Queueable or Batch that implements `Database.AllowsCallouts`, or call a `@future(callout=true)` method.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between Publish After Commit and Publish Immediately?
flashcards.back: After Commit: sent only if the transaction commits. Immediately: sent right away, even if the transaction rolls back.

flashcards.front: Which trigger event works on a platform event, and who runs it?
flashcards.back: Only `after insert`. It runs as the Automated Process user, with up to 2,000 events per batch.

flashcards.front: What does `setResumeCheckpoint` do?
flashcards.back: It saves the Replay ID of the last good event. If the trigger fails, the next run starts right after it. Call `EventBus.TriggerContext.currentContext().setResumeCheckpoint(replayId)`.

flashcards.front: What happens when you throw `EventBus.RetryableException`?
flashcards.back: The platform resends the whole event batch to the trigger. It retries up to 9 times.

flashcards.front: How do you deliver platform events in a test?
flashcards.back: Publish between `Test.startTest()` and `Test.stopTest()`; events are delivered at `stopTest()`. Or call `Test.getEventBus().deliver()` to deliver them right away.

flashcards.front: What are change event objects called?
flashcards.back: Standard: `AccountChangeEvent`. Custom: `MyObj__ChangeEvent`. The channel is `/data/AccountChangeEvent`.

flashcards.front: Which fields does a `ChangeEventHeader` hold?
flashcards.back: `changeType`, `changedFields`, `recordIds`, `entityName`, `commitUser` and `transactionKey`.

flashcards.front: What are the callout limits?
flashcards.back: 100 callouts per transaction. Timeout: default 10 s, max 120 s per callout. Max 120 s of callout time per transaction.

flashcards.front: What causes 'You have uncommitted work pending'?
flashcards.back: A callout made after pending work in the same transaction: DML, queued async Apex (like `@future`), scheduled Apex or sending email. Do the callout first, or move it to async Apex.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a Named and an External Credential?
flashcards.back: Named Credential = the endpoint URL (`callout:Name`). External Credential = the login method plus principals, given to users through permission sets.

flashcards.front: What is a Continuation for?
flashcards.back: A long callout from LWC, Aura or Visualforce without holding a server thread. Up to 3 callouts, 120 s timeout. Use `@AuraEnabled(continuation=true cacheable=true)`.

flashcards.front: What URL does an Apex REST class answer on?
flashcards.back: `/services/apexrest/<urlMapping>`. The class is `global`, and its methods are `global static`.

flashcards.front: How do you build an Apex SOAP web service?
flashcards.back: A `global` class with `webservice static` methods. Callers use the WSDL Salesforce generates for it.

flashcards.front: What are the rules for `@InvocableMethod`?
flashcards.back: One per class. `Static`, `public` or `global`. One List parameter. Returns a List or `void`.

flashcards.front: How do you fix `MIXED_DML_OPERATION`?
flashcards.back: Move the setup-object DML (`User`, `PermissionSetAssignment`, `GroupMember`...) to `@future` or other async Apex. In tests, use `System.runAs`.

flashcards.front: How do you stop SOQL injection?
flashcards.back: Use bind variables, `Database.queryWithBinds` or `String.escapeSingleQuotes`. Check field names against Schema describe results.

flashcards.front: What do unchanged fields look like in an Apex change event?
flashcards.back: They are null. Check `changedFields`, and `nulledFields` for real nulls. One event can list many Ids in `recordIds`.

flashcards.front: Do `transient` fields reach a Transaction Finalizer?
flashcards.back: No. Serialization skips them, so they don't persist. Other fields keep the values they had when the Queueable ended.

questions.q: An admin builds a before-save record-triggered flow on Case that sets Priority. A developer's before insert trigger on Case reads Priority to set an SLA date. In what order do they run?
options: The before trigger runs first, so it always sees the original Priority
The before-save flow runs first, so the trigger sees the Priority the flow set
They run in parallel, so the order cannot be predicted
The flow runs after the after insert trigger, so the trigger never sees its value
questions.explain: Before-save flows always go before before triggers. So the trigger sees the Priority the flow already set.
wrong: Before triggers run after before-save flows, not before them.
Salesforce runs these steps one at a time, in a fixed, documented order.
That describes after-save flows, not before-save flows.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: An after update trigger on Account updates related records. A workflow field update made the trigger fire twice, so the developer added a `static Boolean` `'hasRun'` flag. Now an Apex data fix that runs one `update` on 600 Accounts only processes the first 200. What is the best fix?
options: Reset `hasRun` to false at the end of the before update trigger
Split the trigger into three triggers so each one handles 200 of the 600 Accounts
Swap the Boolean for a `static Set<Id>` and skip only records already in the set
Move the logic to a before update trigger, which only fires once per transaction
questions.explain: One DML statement with 600 records runs the trigger three times (200 per chunk) in one transaction. A `static Boolean` stays true after chunk 1, so chunks 2 and 3 are skipped. A `static Set<Id>` remembers each record, so new records in later chunks still get processed.
wrong: The flag would still be shared by every chunk, and the timing gets messy fast.
Several triggers on one event run in no set order, and every one of them still sees all three chunks and the same shared flag.
Workflow field updates fire before update triggers again too.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution; Bulk Triggers

questions.q: Which two steps run AFTER the after triggers in the save order of execution? (Choose 2)
options: Assignment rules
Before-save record-triggered flows
Custom validation rules
Roll-up summary calculation on the parent record
Duplicate rules
questions.explain: After triggers run right after the record is saved. Then come assignment, auto-response, workflow and escalation rules, then after-save flows, then roll-up summaries on the parent. Before-save flows, custom validation rules and duplicate rules all run before the save, so before after triggers.
wrong: These run before the before triggers.
These run after before triggers but before the record is saved.
Duplicate rules run before the save, so before after triggers.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: A developer must set `Region__c` on Lead based on the Lead's State whenever a Lead is created. Which approach uses the fewest resources?
options: An after insert trigger that queries the Leads and calls `update`
A Queueable job enqueued from an after insert trigger
A scheduled job that fixes `Region__c` every hour
A before insert trigger that sets `Region__c` on the records in `Trigger.new`
questions.explain: Changing a field in a before trigger is free. Edits to `Trigger.new` save with the record, with no extra query or DML.
wrong: It needs extra SOQL and DML, and the update fires triggers again.
Async adds a delay and a second transaction for a simple same-record change.
The data stays wrong for up to an hour, and it wastes resources.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Trigger Context Variables

questions.q: A team has three before update triggers on Opportunity written by different developers. Behaviour changes unpredictably between releases. What should the architect recommend?
options: One trigger per object that delegates to a handler class controlling the order
Set the trigger execution order in Setup > Apex Triggers so each trigger runs in a fixed rank
Convert all three triggers to after update triggers
Put each trigger's logic in a separate `@future` method
questions.explain: Salesforce does not promise any order for several triggers on the same object and event. One trigger with a handler class puts the order in your hands.
wrong: Setup has no option to order Apex triggers.
The order is still not guaranteed, and same-record updates cost more.
It adds async work and doesn't fix the order.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers; Trailhead: Apex Triggers best practices

questions.q: A nightly integration inserts 1,000 Contacts with `Database.insert(contacts, false)`. A before insert trigger calls `addError()` on 3 records with invalid emails. What happens?
options: All 1,000 records are rolled back and a `DmlException` is thrown
The 3 records are saved but flagged with a warning
997 records save; the 3 fail and their errors are in the `SaveResults`
The trigger skips the 3 records and saves them without the email field
questions.explain: With `allOrNone` set to false, each record stands alone. The 3 records marked with `addError` fail, and the other 997 save. Each failure is in its `SaveResult`.
wrong: That only happens with plain `insert` or `allOrNone = true`.
`addError` blocks the save; it is not a warning.
`addError` doesn't strip fields; it fails the whole record.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: SObject addError; Database.SaveResult

questions.q: This trigger works in testing but fails with 'Too many SOQL queries: 101' during a 200-record data load. What is the best refactor?
options: Wrap the query in a try/catch so the `LimitException` is handled
Collect AccountIds in a Set, query once into a `Map<Id, Account>`, then look up each one
Move the query into an `@future` method called once per Case so each call gets its own SOQL limit
Add `LIMIT 1` to the query so each query costs less
questions.explain: Never query inside a loop. Collect the Account Ids, query them once into a Map, then look each one up. That uses 1 SOQL query however many records come in.
wrong: A `LimitException` can't be caught.
Before triggers can't change records from async code, and 200 future calls pass the limit of 50.
`LIMIT` makes each query smaller but doesn't cut the number of queries.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A developer wants a custom exception to throw when a payment fails. Which declaration compiles?
options: `public class PaymentError extends Exception {}`
`public class PaymentException implements Exception {}`
`public exception PaymentException {}`
`public class PaymentException extends Exception {}`
questions.explain: A custom exception is a class that extends the built-in `Exception` class. Apex also requires its name to end with 'Exception'. Only option D does both; you then throw it with `throw new PaymentException('message');`.
wrong: The name must end with 'Exception'.
`Exception` is a class you extend, not an interface you implement.
Apex has no 'exception' type keyword.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Create Custom Exceptions

questions.q: A developer must pass a `List<Opportunity>` with in-memory changes to asynchronous code. Which option supports this?
options: An `@future` method with a `List<Opportunity>` parameter
An `@future` method with a `Map<Id, Opportunity>` parameter
A class that implements Queueable and stores the list in a member variable
A Schedulable class that takes the list in its execute method
questions.explain: Future methods accept only primitives and collections of primitives, so any parameter holding sObjects (List or Map) won't compile. A Queueable keeps sObjects and other complex types in member variables, so the in-memory changes travel with the job.
wrong: Future methods can't take sObjects.
A Map of sObjects isn't allowed either.
Schedulable `execute()` only takes a `SchedulableContext`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Future Methods; Queueable Apex

questions.q: Inside an executing Queueable job, a developer calls `System.enqueueJob()` in a loop to start 3 follow-up jobs. What happens?
options: The second call throws a `LimitException`: an executing Queueable can enqueue only one child job
All three jobs run in parallel
All three jobs run in order, one after another
The `enqueueJob()` calls are ignored until the parent job commits, and then only the last enqueued job actually runs
questions.explain: An executing Queueable may add only one job to the queue. The second `enqueueJob` call throws a `LimitException`. To run more work, chain: each job enqueues the next.
wrong: The second enqueue fails, so nothing runs in parallel.
Only one child is allowed. Chain the jobs one by one instead.
The limit throws an exception; the calls are not quietly ignored.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex (Chaining Jobs); Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A Queueable must call an external API, wait at least 5 minutes before it starts (to let the remote system catch up), and not be enqueued twice for the same record. Which two actions should the developer take? (Choose 2)
options: Use `@future(callout=true, delay=5)`
Have the Queueable class implement `Database.AllowsCallouts`
Enqueue with `AsyncOptions`, setting `MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes` to 5 and a `DuplicateSignature` built from the record Id
Call a busy-wait loop for 5 minutes at the start of `execute()`
Schedule a Schedulable class for 5 minutes from now with a callout in its execute method
questions.explain: A Queueable needs `Database.AllowsCallouts` to make callouts. `AsyncOptions` adds the rest: a minimum delay and a duplicate signature that blocks a second identical job.
wrong: `@future` has no delay attribute.
A wait loop burns CPU time and would hit limits.
Scheduled Apex can't make synchronous callouts.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex; AsyncOptions Class

questions.q: An Account trigger calls an `@future` method to sync data. A new Batch Apex job updates Accounts and fails with 'Future method cannot be called from a future or batch method'. What is the best fix?
options: Add `Database.Stateful` to the batch class
Call `Database.executeBatch(job, 1)` so each `execute()` handles one Account and the trigger makes only one future call
Add `@future` to the batch execute method
In the handler, skip the `@future` call when `System.isBatch()` or `System.isFuture()` is true (or use a Queueable)
questions.explain: Future methods can't be called from batch or future code. Check `System.isBatch()` or `System.isFuture()` and take another path, such as a Queueable.
wrong: Keeping state has nothing to do with this error.
It is still batch context whatever the scope, so the future call is still blocked.
Batch interface methods can't be future methods.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Future Methods; System Class

questions.q: A Queueable job sometimes fails with an uncatchable limit exception. Its DML is rolled back, but the team still needs a log record saying which job failed. What should the developer use?
options: A try/catch block around the whole execute method
A class implementing `Finalizer`, attached with `System.attachFinalizer()` inside `execute()`
A `Database.Stateful` variable that stores the error
A Savepoint created at the start of `execute()`
questions.explain: You need code that runs after the job, even when it crashes. A Transaction Finalizer runs in its own transaction after the Queueable ends, so it can read the error and save a log.
wrong: Limit exceptions can't be caught.
`Database.Stateful` is for Batch Apex, and the state would be lost on failure anyway.
Savepoints don't help after an uncaught exception, and the log needs its own transaction.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: A Finalizer re-enqueues its Queueable whenever the result is `UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`. The external system is down for an hour, so every attempt fails. What does the platform do?
options: It retries forever until the job succeeds
It blocks the first re-enqueue, because finalizers can't enqueue jobs
It allows up to 5 consecutive re-enqueues of the failing job, then stops
It suspends all Queueable jobs in the org for 24 hours
questions.explain: The platform caps retries from a finalizer. A Queueable that keeps failing can be re-enqueued up to 5 consecutive times, then it stops. Add your own retry count and alerts.
wrong: There is a cap on consecutive failed re-enqueues, so it never retries forever.
Finalizers can enqueue one async job.
Salesforce has no org-wide Queueable suspension like that.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers (Limits)

questions.q: How many Transaction Finalizers can be attached to one Queueable job?
options: One
Two: one for success and one for failure
Up to 5
Up to 50
questions.explain: Only one finalizer can be attached to each Queueable job; attaching a second throws an error. That's enough, because the one finalizer runs on success and failure alike and checks `getResult()` to tell which happened.
wrong: One finalizer handles both outcomes.
Only one finalizer is allowed.
Only one finalizer is allowed.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: A Batch Apex job must email a summary of how many records failed across all chunks. The count is always 0 in `finish()`. What should the developer change?
options: Make the counter a `static` variable
Increase the batch scope to 2,000
Write the counter to a Custom Label
Implement `Database.Stateful` and keep the counter as an instance variable
questions.explain: Each chunk of a batch is a fresh transaction, so normal variables reset. `Database.Stateful` keeps instance variables between chunks, so the counter reaches `finish()`.
wrong: Static variables reset in every batch transaction.
Fewer chunks would still lose the count; it does not fix state.
Apex can't update Custom Labels at run time.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using State in Batch Apex

questions.q: A batch must process about 8 million Task records selected by a simple SOQL filter. What should `start()` return?
options: An `Iterable<Task>` built from a SOQL query
A `Database.QueryLocator`
A `List<Task>` from a SOQL query
A `Database.Cursor` holding the query
questions.explain: For millions of simple rows, use a `QueryLocator`. It can return up to 50 million records. An `Iterable` is held to the normal SOQL row limit of 50,000.
wrong: An `Iterable` `start()` is bound by the 50,000 query-row limit.
A List is an `Iterable`, so it hits the same row limit.
Batch `start()` takes a `QueryLocator` or an `Iterable`, not a cursor.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex

questions.q: Every night at 1 AM an org must send updated prices to an ERP REST API. Which two designs work? (Choose 2)
options: A Schedulable class whose `execute()` builds the `HttpRequest` and makes the ERP callout directly with `Http.send()`
A Schedulable class that starts a Batch Apex job implementing `Database.AllowsCallouts`
A Schedulable class that enqueues a Queueable implementing `Database.AllowsCallouts`
Set `callout=true` on the Schedulable class's execute method
An after update trigger on Pricebook entries that waits until 1 AM
questions.explain: Scheduled Apex can't make synchronous callouts, so its `execute()` must hand the work to async code that may call out. A Batch or Queueable class that implements `Database.AllowsCallouts` does exactly that, and the schedule still decides the 1 AM start.
wrong: Scheduled Apex doesn't support synchronous callouts.
Schedulable has no callout attribute.
Triggers can't wait for a time of day.

questions.q: Which cron expression runs a scheduled Apex job every day at 2:00 AM?
questions.explain: Apex cron starts with seconds, then minutes, then hours. So `'0 0 2 * * ?'` means 02:00:00 every day.
wrong: This is 5-field Unix cron. Apex cron needs seconds first.

questions.q: A developer needs async processing that takes a list of sObjects as input, returns a job Id to show progress in the UI, and can start a follow-up job when done. Which tool fits best?

Schedulable Apex

A platform event

questions.q: Every Sunday an org must recalculate a score on 3 million Contact records. Which solution is most appropriate?
options: A Queueable that loops through all Contacts in one `execute()`
An `@future` method called once a week by a user
A record-triggered flow on Contact
A Batch Apex class started by a Schedulable class

questions.q: When an Opportunity is Closed Won, the order must be sent to a fulfilment REST API. The developer adds an HTTP callout inside the after update trigger and gets 'Callout from triggers are currently not supported'. What should they do?
options: Move the callout to the before update trigger
Enqueue a Queueable that implements `Database.AllowsCallouts`, passing the Opportunity Ids
Use a Savepoint before the callout
Wrap the callout in `Test.isRunningTest()` checks
questions.explain: Triggers can't make synchronous callouts. Hand the work to async Apex that allows callouts, like a Queueable with `Database.AllowsCallouts`. Pass Ids, not records.
wrong: No trigger context allows synchronous callouts.

That check only changes tests, not production.

questions.q: Five batch jobs are already running. A user starts a sixth with `Database.executeBatch()`. What happens?
options: The job goes into the Apex flex queue in Holding status until a slot frees up
An exception is thrown and the job is lost
The oldest running batch is aborted
The job runs synchronously instead
questions.explain: Only 5 batch jobs can be queued or active at once. Extra jobs wait in the Apex flex queue as Holding, up to 100 of them.
wrong: The flex queue holds the job (up to 100), so nothing is lost.
Running jobs are never stopped to make room.
Batch jobs never run synchronously.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex (Apex Flex Queue)

questions.q: A developer wants an error log written even when the transaction that hit the error rolls back. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Insert a custom `Error_Log__c` record in the catch block
Publish a platform event set to Publish After Commit and insert the log from its trigger
Use `System.debug`, which is persisted on rollback
Publish a platform event set to Publish Immediately and insert the log from its subscriber
questions.explain: A rollback undoes all normal DML, so the log must leave the transaction first. Publish Immediately events go out at once and survive the rollback. A subscriber saves the log in its own transaction.
wrong: That insert is rolled back with everything else.
After Commit events are thrown away when the transaction rolls back.
Debug logs aren't data and aren't always captured.

questions.q: Which trigger events are supported on a platform event object like `Payment_Received__e`?
options: `before insert` and `after insert`
`after insert` only
`after insert` and `after update`
All DML events, like custom objects
questions.explain: Once published, an event can't change. So platform event triggers support only `after insert`.
wrong: `before insert` is not supported.
Events can't be updated, so there is no `after update`.
Only `after insert` is supported.

questions.q: A platform event trigger gets batches of up to 2,000 events. Sometimes it hits CPU limits partway through, and events already processed are processed again on retry. How should the developer resume from the last good event?
options: Use a static variable to remember the last processed event
Query the Platform Event object with SOQL for events already processed in this batch and skip them
Call `setResumeCheckpoint(event.ReplayId)` on `EventBus.TriggerContext` after each event
Throw a `DmlException` so the platform skips the batch
questions.explain: `setResumeCheckpoint` saves your place in the batch. It stores the Replay ID of the last good event. If the trigger fails, the next run starts with the event after it.
wrong: Static variables don't survive between trigger runs.

An unhandled exception doesn't skip events in a controlled way.

questions.q: A test publishes `Order_Shipped__e` and asserts that its trigger created a Task. The assertion fails because the trigger hasn't run yet. Which two changes make the event deliver during the test? (Choose 2)
options: Publish between `Test.startTest()` and `Test.stopTest()`, then assert after `stopTest()`
Call `EventBus.flush()` after publishing
Insert the event with a normal `insert` statement
Add `@isTest(SeeAllData=true)`
Call `Test.getEventBus().deliver()` after publishing
questions.explain: In tests, events wait until you deliver them. `Test.stopTest()` delivers events published after `startTest()`. `Test.getEventBus().deliver()` delivers them on demand.
wrong: `EventBus.flush()` doesn't exist.
Events are published with `EventBus.publish`, and delivery still waits.
Access to org data doesn't change event delivery.

questions.q: By default, which user does a platform event Apex trigger run as?
options: The Automated Process user
The user who published the event
The org's default workflow user
A system administrator chosen at random
questions.explain: Event triggers run apart from the publisher. By default they run as the Automated Process user. `PlatformEventSubscriberConfig` can set a different user and batch size.
wrong: The trigger runs separately from the publisher's transaction.
That user is for some workflow actions, not event triggers.
Salesforce never picks a user at random.
