questions.q: A data warehouse must get near real-time notice of every create, update, delete and undelete on Account, with no new Apex written in Salesforce. What should the developer set up?
options: An Account trigger that publishes a custom platform event with `EventBus.publish()`
Outbound messages from a workflow rule
Enable Change Data Capture for Account; the warehouse subscribes to `/data/AccountChangeEvent`
A scheduled Batch Apex job that exports Accounts changed since its last run to the warehouse every hour
questions.explain: Change Data Capture needs no code. Turn it on for Account and Salesforce sends an event for every create, update, delete and undelete. The warehouse subscribes to the channel.
wrong: It needs custom code and misses changes the trigger's logic doesn't cover.

questions.q: A CDC Apex trigger on `AccountChangeEvent` should act only when `BillingCountry` changed on an update. How does the developer check this?
options: Compare `Trigger.oldMap.get(recordId).BillingCountry` against the value in `Trigger.new` for each event
Check `ChangeEventHeader.changeType` and whether its `changedFields` contains `'BillingCountry'`
Query `AccountHistory` for the record in the trigger
Use the `ISCHANGED()` function in Apex
questions.explain: The change event header says what changed. Check `changeType` for `UPDATE`, then see if `changedFields` contains `BillingCountry`. Change event triggers have no `Trigger.old`.
wrong: Change event triggers are after insert on the event, so there is no `Trigger.old`.
Field history may not be tracked, and it costs a query.
ISCHANGED is a formula function, not Apex.

questions.q: Which two statements correctly compare Change Data Capture with custom platform events? (Choose 2)
options: Both require the developer to call `EventBus.publish`
CDC events can be published with Publish Immediately so they survive rollbacks
Platform events support before insert triggers, while CDC does not
CDC events are generated automatically when records of selected objects change
Custom platform events have a schema the developer defines with custom fields
questions.explain: CDC events are made by the platform from committed record changes. Custom platform events are messages whose fields you define and publish yourself.
wrong: CDC needs no publish call.
CDC events are only published after commit.

questions.q: A Lightning controller inserts an `Order__c` and then makes an HTTP callout to a tax service in the same method. It throws 'You have uncommitted work pending'. What is the best fix?
options: Make the callout first, then insert the record with the tax result
Add a Savepoint before the callout
Increase the callout timeout to 120 seconds
Add the endpoint to Remote Site Settings
questions.explain: You can't make a callout after DML in the same transaction. Call out first, then save the record with the tax result, or move the callout to async Apex.
wrong: A savepoint doesn't commit the work, so it is still pending.
The timeout has nothing to do with this error.
A missing remote site gives a different error.

questions.q: A developer must call an OAuth-protected partner API without storing the endpoint or secrets in code, and only users in the Partner Sync permission set may use it. Which two steps are needed? (Choose 2)

Create a Named Credential that references the External Credential and use `'callout:Partner_API/...'` as the endpoint
Add the user's password to the endpoint URL in a Remote Site Setting
Store the OAuth token in a protected custom metadata type field and add it as an Authorization header in Apex
questions.explain: Keep the URL and the login out of code. The Named Credential holds the URL, and the External Credential holds the OAuth setup. Users get its principal through the permission set.
wrong: Custom Labels aren't a secure place for secrets.

Handling tokens yourself isn't needed and is less safe.

60 seconds
120 seconds
10 minutes

wrong: You can set more than 30 seconds.

Return a Continuation from an `@AuraEnabled(continuation=true)` method and handle the response in a callback
Set the callout timeout to 5 seconds and retry in a loop
Move the callout into the component's JavaScript with `fetch()`
questions.explain: A long callout shouldn't tie up a server thread. A Continuation runs it in the background, then a callback sends the result back to the component.

wrong: Tests can't make real callouts, whatever the data access setting.

Expose the operations with the `webservice` keyword

`/apex/shipments/`
`/services/apexrest/shipments/`

A `global` class with a `webservice static` method; share the generated WSDL
An `@InvocableMethod` in an Apex class, which the partner calls through the REST Actions API
An outbound message sent from a flow

`public static String lookup(Id recordId)`
`public static List<String> lookup(List<Id> ids)`
`global static List<String> lookup(List<Id> ids, String mode)`

questions.q: A record-triggered flow on Order calls an invocable action. When 200 Orders are loaded, the action fails with too many SOQL queries. What is the most likely cause?
options: Invocable methods have a lower SOQL limit of 20
Flow calls the invocable method 200 separate times, each in its own parallel transaction
Order needs a before-save flow instead
Flow passes all 200 Ids in one call, so the query in the loop runs 200 times
questions.explain: Flow bundles its interviews into one call. All 200 Ids arrive in one List, so the query in the loop runs 200 times. Query once, outside the loop.
wrong: Normal transaction limits apply; there is no special limit of 20.
Flow batches the interviews into one call with a 200-item list.
Changing the flow type doesn't fix Apex that isn't bulkified.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableMethod Annotation; Salesforce Help: Flow Bulkification

questions.q: An invocable action needs three inputs from a flow: an Account Id, a discount and a reason. How should the developer define them?
options: An inner class with three `@InvocableVariable` fields, and `List<ThatClass>` as the parameter
Add three parameters to the `@InvocableMethod`
Pass a `Map<String, Object>` parameter
Add three `@InvocableMethod` methods to one class, one per input, and Flow calls them in order
questions.explain: An invocable method takes only one parameter. So bundle the inputs in an inner class with `@InvocableVariable` fields, and take a List of that class.
wrong: Only one parameter is allowed.
Maps aren't supported as invocable inputs.
Only one `@InvocableMethod` is allowed per class.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableVariable Annotation

questions.q: Which two statements about `@InvocableMethod` are true? (Choose 2)
options: Only one method per class can have the annotation
The method can be an instance method if the class has a constructor
The method must be `static` and either `public` or `global`
The method can accept up to three parameters
The method must return a Map
questions.explain: Each class can have one invocable method. It must be `static`, `public` or `global`, and take a single List parameter.
wrong: It must be `static`.
Only one parameter is allowed.
It returns a List or `void`, not a Map.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableMethod Annotation

questions.q: An import job must save every valid Lead and write failed rows with their error messages to a log object. Which two steps should the developer take? (Choose 2)
options: Use `insert leads;` inside `try/catch(DmlException e)`
Call `Database.insert(leads, false)`
Use `Database.insert(leads, true)`
Loop the returned `Database.SaveResult` list and read `getErrors()` where `isSuccess()` is false
Check `Limits.getDmlRows()` after the insert
questions.explain: To keep the good rows, allow partial success. `Database.insert(leads, false)` saves the valid rows. Each `SaveResult` lines up with its input row and holds its errors.
wrong: Plain `insert` is all-or-nothing, so one bad row rolls back every row.
`true` means all-or-nothing.
That counts rows; it doesn't report errors.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Database Class Methods; SaveResult Class

questions.q: When a `Partner_Account__c` is approved, Apex updates the record and inserts a `PermissionSetAssignment` for the partner's user in the same transaction. It fails with `MIXED_DML_OPERATION`. What should the developer do?
options: Use `Database.insert` with `allOrNone = false` for the `PermissionSetAssignment`
Wrap both operations in `System.runAs()` in production code
Move the `PermissionSetAssignment` insert to an `@future` method that takes the Ids
Insert the `PermissionSetAssignment` before the custom object update in the same transaction
questions.explain: Setup objects (like `PermissionSetAssignment`) and normal objects can't be changed in the same transaction, in any order. An `@future` method runs in a separate transaction, so pass it the Ids and insert the assignment there. `System.runAs` is only for tests, and partial success doesn't avoid the error.
wrong: Partial success doesn't avoid mixed DML.
`System.runAs` only works in test methods.
The order within one transaction doesn't matter.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: sObjects That Cannot Be Used Together in DML Operations

questions.q: A search page builds this query from user input. Which two changes prevent SOQL injection? (Choose 2)
options: Use a bind variable: `'WHERE LastName = :searchText'`
Add `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` to the query
Trim whitespace from `searchText`
Wrap the input with `String.escapeSingleQuotes(searchText)`
Run the query in a `without sharing` class
questions.explain: Treat user input as data, never as part of the query. A bind variable does that. `escapeSingleQuotes` stops the input from breaking out of the quoted string.
wrong: It enforces field-level security but doesn't stop injection.
Trimming doesn't remove quotes or operators.
It widens access and makes the risk worse.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: SOQL Injection; Dynamic SOQL

questions.q: An ERP sends Accounts with an `ERP_Number__c` external Id field. The developer must create new Accounts or update existing ones, and report which rows were new. Which code fits?
options: `Database.insert(accts, false)`, then check each `SaveResult`'s `isCreated()` and update the rows that failed
`upsert accts;` then query `CreatedDate`
`Database.merge(accts, ERP_Number__c)`
`Database.upsert(accts, Account.ERP_Number__c, false)`, then check each `UpsertResult`'s `isCreated()`
questions.explain: Upsert with an external Id field finds matching records by that field. Each `UpsertResult` has `isCreated()`, which says whether the row was new.
wrong: Insert never updates, and `SaveResult` has no `isCreated()`.
Without the field, `upsert` matches on Salesforce Id, and the extra query is wasteful.
`merge` combines duplicate records; it isn't an upsert.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Database.upsert; UpsertResult Class

questions.q: A method inserts an `Invoice__c` and then its line items. If any line item fails, the invoice must be removed too, but the method should catch the error and not throw. What should the developer use?
options: A `@future` method for the line items
`Database.insert` with `allOrNone = false` for both
`Savepoint sp = Database.setSavepoint();` then `Database.rollback(sp)` in the catch block
Delete the invoice in a finally block every time
questions.explain: A savepoint is an undo point inside one transaction. `Database.rollback(sp)` undoes all DML since then, so the invoice and its lines go together. Catching the error keeps the method from throwing.
wrong: It splits the work into separate transactions, so the invoice stays.
Partial success keeps the invoice.
That deletes the invoice even when everything worked.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: A finalizer writes a log when its Queueable fails. Support wants to open the matching `AsyncApexJob` record from the log. Which value should the finalizer store?
options: `ctx.getRequestId()`, which is the `AsyncApexJob` record's Id
`ctx.getAsyncApexJobId()`, the Id of the Queueable job
`UserInfo.getSessionId()` of the user who enqueued the job
`ctx.getException().getStackTraceString()` for the failed job
questions.explain: To open the job record, store the job Id. `getAsyncApexJobId()` returns the Queueable's Id, which matches `AsyncApexJob`. `getRequestId()` is for Event Monitoring logs.
wrong: `getRequestId()` is for Event Monitoring; it isn't the `AsyncApexJob` Id.
A session Id isn't a job Id, and async jobs don't run in that user's session.
A stack trace explains the failure but doesn't point to the job record.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: When an Opportunity is Closed Won, a Slack notifier and an ERP sync (owned by two other teams and changed often) must both react. The Opportunity code shouldn't change when a team adds or removes a reaction. What should the developer use?
options: A Schedulable class that polls each hour for Opportunities that were recently Closed Won
One Queueable, enqueued by the trigger, that calls each team's class one after another
An `@future` method for each team, each one called directly from the Opportunity trigger
Publish a `Deal_Won__e` platform event; each team subscribes with its own trigger or flow
questions.explain: The sender shouldn't know who is listening. A platform event does that. The Opportunity code publishes once, and each team adds or removes its own subscriber.
wrong: Polling isn't near real time, and the job still has to know every team.
The trigger code would still change whenever a team adds or removes a reaction.
The trigger still has to know every team's method.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide

questions.q: Change Data Capture is enabled for the custom object `Invoice__c`. What is the name of its change event?
options: `InvoiceChangeEvent__e`
Invoice__c_ChangeEvent
`Invoice__ChangeEvent`
`Invoice__e`
questions.explain: For a custom object, swap `__c` for `__ChangeEvent`. So `Invoice__c` becomes `Invoice__ChangeEvent`. Standard objects just add ChangeEvent, like `AccountChangeEvent`.
wrong: Change events don't use the `__e` suffix of custom platform events.
The `__c` is replaced, not kept: the name is `Invoice__ChangeEvent`.
`__e` is the suffix for custom platform events, not change events.
questions.source: Change Data Capture Developer Guide: Change Event Object Name

questions.q: A flow calls a weather service and must keep the result (city, temperature, forecast date) in one structured variable it can pass between elements. What should the developer write?
options: A class with `public` `@AuraEnabled` fields, used as an Apex-defined variable in the flow
A class whose `public` fields are marked `@InvocableMethod` so the flow can read them
A `Map<String, Object>` returned by an invocable method and stored in a flow variable
A single Text variable holding JSON, read by flow formulas that parse out each value
questions.explain: Flow can hold a variable shaped like an Apex class. That Apex-defined type is a class with `@AuraEnabled` fields, and Flow can read or set each one.
wrong: `@InvocableMethod` marks one method per class, not fields.
Flow can't store a `Map<String, Object>` in a variable.
Flow formulas can't parse JSON, so the values couldn't be read.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Apex-Defined Data Type in Flow; LWC Developer Guide: Supported Data Types in Flows

questions.q: A support manager wants every Account that had at least one Task created this week. A developer adds this query to a service class. What is the result?
options: It returns the Accounts, plus any Accounts reached through Tasks on their Opportunities
It is valid but returns no rows, because `WhatId` is polymorphic and the subquery must also filter `What.Type = 'Account'`
The query is rejected as invalid SOQL, because Task isn't supported as the object of a semi-join subquery
It is rejected because date literals such as `THIS_WEEK` can't be used inside a subquery
questions.explain: Some objects can't sit inside a semi-join subquery. Task, Event, Note, Attachments and ActivityHistory are among them, so this query is invalid. Query the Tasks first, collect the `WhatId` values in a Set, then query the Accounts.
wrong: Semi-joins match the Id field directly, nothing is reached through Opportunities, and the query isn't valid anyway.
The problem is the subquery object, not the polymorphic field.
Date literals are allowed in a subquery `WHERE` clause.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: Comparison Operators

questions.q: A developer is reviewing queries written by a junior teammate for a renewal dashboard. Which two queries are valid SOQL? (Choose 2)
options: `SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE AccountId IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity WHERE IsWon = true)`
`SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id IN (SELECT ParentId FROM Account WHERE Industry = 'Energy')`
`SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity ORDER BY Amount DESC LIMIT 5)`
`SELECT Id, (SELECT Id FROM Contacts) FROM Account WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Case WHERE IsClosed = false)`
`SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE Account.Id IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Case)`
questions.explain: A semi-join can match two reference fields, like `Contact.AccountId` to `Opportunity.AccountId`. An anti-join can also sit in the `WHERE` clause of a query with a parent-child subquery.
wrong: A semi-join can't query the same object as the main query; use `WHERE Parent.Industry` instead.
`ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, `COUNT` and `FOR UPDATE` aren't allowed in semi-join subqueries.
The left side of a semi-join can't use a relationship like `Account.Id`; it must be a plain Id or reference field.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: Comparison Operators

questions.q: A nightly job emails partner managers. One partner Account has 450 Contacts. The code below sometimes fails on that Account. What is the cause and the fix?
options: Reading `acct.Contacts` whole (or its `size()`) can throw 'Aggregate query has too many rows'; use an inner for loop
Subqueries silently return only the first 200 children; add `LIMIT 500` to the subquery
The query exceeds the 50,000 query-row limit; move the logic to Batch Apex
SOQL for loops can't contain parent-child subqueries; split it into two queries and join them with a `Map<Id, List<Contact>>`
questions.explain: Inside a SOQL for loop, don't grab a big child list all at once. Assigning or sizing 200 or more children can throw 'Aggregate query has too many rows'. An inner for loop over `acct.Contacts` fetches them in chunks.
wrong: Children aren't quietly cut off; the error comes from reading a big child set all at once.
450 Contacts is far below 50,000 rows; this is a `QueryException`, not the row limit.
Parent-child subqueries are allowed in SOQL for loops; the problem is how the child list is read.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: SOQL For Loops

questions.q: A service dashboard controller runs these three queries. The org has 30,000 open Cases owned by 40 different users. How many rows count toward the 50,000 query-row limit?
options: 90,000, so the third query throws a `LimitException`
questions.explain: Each aggregate counts rows differently. `COUNT()` with no `GROUP BY` counts as 1 row. Grouped `COUNT(Id)` counts one per group (40). `SUM()` counts every row it adds up (30,000), so the total is 30,041.
wrong: `SUM()` counts every row it adds up, not one row per result.
Rows are counted per record or group used, not per query.
`COUNT()` and grouped `COUNT(Id)` don't count every record, so the total stays under 50,000.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with SOQL Aggregate Functions

questions.q: A sales report loops over this query. The data has 3 regions, and each region sold exactly 2 product lines (6 combinations, no null values). How many rows does the loop process, and how does the code spot the grand total row?
options: 6 rows; subtotals must be added up in Apex
10 rows; the grand total row has `gR = 1` and `gP = 1`
9 rows; the grand total row has `gR = 0` and `gP = 0`
12 rows (6 detail, 3 region, 2 product, 1 grand total); the grand total row has `gR = 1` and `gP = 1`
questions.explain: `ROLLUP` adds subtotal rows on top of the detail rows. Here that is 6 details, 3 region subtotals and 1 grand total: 10 rows. `GROUPING(field)` is 1 on a subtotal for that field, so the grand total has both flags at 1.
wrong: `ROLLUP` adds subtotal and grand total rows to the detail rows.
`GROUPING` returns 1, not 0, on subtotal rows, and this count misses the grand total.
Subtotals for every combination of fields come from `GROUP BY CUBE`, not `ROLLUP`.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: GROUP BY ROLLUP; GROUPING(fieldName)

questions.q: Two warehouse users sometimes reserve the last unit of the same product at the same moment. A developer adds `FOR UPDATE` to the reservation query below, but the query now fails. Why?
questions.code:
List<Inventory__c> stock = [
    SELECT Id, On_Hand__c FROM Inventory__c
    WHERE Product__c = :productId
    ORDER BY CreatedDate
    FOR UPDATE];
options: `FOR UPDATE` must come before the `WHERE` clause
`FOR UPDATE` can only be used in classes declared `without sharing`
`ORDER BY` isn't allowed with `FOR UPDATE`; remove it and sort in Apex
`FOR UPDATE` needs a `LIMIT` clause so the platform knows how many rows to lock
questions.explain: A locking query can't sort its rows. Remove `ORDER BY` and sort in Apex. `FOR UPDATE` itself is in the right place, at the end.
wrong: `FOR UPDATE` goes at the end of the query, after `WHERE`.
Sharing keywords have nothing to do with record locking.
`LIMIT` is optional; `FOR UPDATE` locks every row the query returns.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Locking Statements

questions.q: A reservation method locks the Inventory rows, calls an external pricing API, then updates the stock. Under load, the stock is still sometimes oversold. What is the most likely reason?
options: A callout releases the `FOR UPDATE` locks, so another transaction can change the rows before the update
`FOR UPDATE` locks expire after 10 seconds, and the pricing API takes longer than that
`FOR UPDATE` only blocks edits from the user interface, not from other Apex transactions
The callout throws 'uncommitted work pending' because a lock counts as pending DML, so the update is skipped
questions.explain: A callout lets go of your locks. The platform releases `FOR UPDATE` locks when a callout is made and logs `FOR_UPDATE_LOCKS_RELEASE`. Call out first, then lock, re-read and update.
wrong: 10 seconds is how long another transaction waits for a lock; the lock itself lasts until the transaction ends.
Locked records are blocked for every other client, code and UI alike.
A lock isn't pending DML; the callout is allowed, it just releases the locks.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Locking Statements

questions.q: An order desk uses `FOR UPDATE` to stop two agents from editing the same `Order__c` record at once. Which two statements about these locks are true? (Choose 2)
options: The locks are released as soon as the SOQL statement finishes running
Another transaction that tries to lock the same rows waits up to 10 seconds and then gets a `QueryException`
`FOR UPDATE` in a Batch Apex `start()` method keeps the records locked across every `execute()` chunk
The transaction that locked the records can't update them until it commits
Other users can still query the locked records while they are locked
questions.explain: A `FOR UPDATE` lock lasts until the transaction ends. Another transaction that wants the same lock waits up to 10 seconds, then gets a `QueryException`. Plain reads still work.
wrong: Locks are released when the transaction ends, not when the query ends.
`FOR UPDATE` doesn't apply to Batch Apex; each chunk is its own transaction. To lock records, requery them with `FOR UPDATE` inside `execute()`.
The transaction holding the lock can update the records; that is the point of the lock.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Locking Statements; Use Batch Apex

questions.q: A daily digest totals today's open pipeline from Tasks. Tasks can relate to Accounts or Opportunities. What happens when this code runs?
options: It doesn't compile, because `TYPEOF` can only be used in dynamic SOQL
It fails at the cast, because a polymorphic `What` field can only be read as the `Name` object
It doesn't compile, because a `TYPEOF` expression must include an `ELSE` clause
It works: `TYPEOF` returns type-specific fields, and `instanceof` plus a cast reads Amount from the related Opportunity
questions.explain: `TYPEOF` picks different fields based on the related record's type. In Apex, `instanceof` checks the real type of `t.What`, so the cast to Opportunity is safe.
wrong: `TYPEOF` works in inline SOQL in Apex.
The related record comes back as its real type, so `instanceof` and a cast work.
`ELSE` is optional in `TYPEOF`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with Polymorphic Relationships in SOQL Queries; SOQL and SOSL Reference: TYPEOF

questions.q: A report must show only Events whose related record (`What`) is an Account, not an Opportunity or Campaign. Which two WHERE clauses on an Event query return exactly those Events? (Choose 2)
options: `WHERE TYPEOF What WHEN Account THEN true END`
`WHERE What instanceof Account`
`WHERE What.Type = 'Account'`
`WHERE WhatId != null GROUP BY TYPEOF What`
`WHERE WhatId IN (SELECT Id FROM Account)`
questions.explain: To filter a polymorphic field by type, use the `Type` qualifier. A semi-join that limits `WhatId` to Account Ids works too.
wrong: `TYPEOF` is only allowed in the `SELECT` clause.
`instanceof` is an Apex operator, not SOQL.
`TYPEOF` can't be used with `GROUP BY`, and grouping doesn't filter by type anyway.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: TYPEOF; Comparison Operators

questions.q: A service lead asks for every Case created 'in the last 7 days', and wants to know whether today's Cases are included. Which records does this query return?
options: Cases from the 7 full days before today; today's Cases are excluded
From midnight 7 days ago until now, so today is included (8 calendar days)
Cases created in the last 168 hours (7 × 24), counted back from the current date and time
None: date literals can't be compared to DateTime fields with =
questions.explain: `LAST_N_DAYS` counts today too. `LAST_N_DAYS:7` starts at midnight 7 days before today and runs up to now, so today is included. `LAST_N_DAYS:1` means yesterday and today.
wrong: `LAST_N_DAYS` includes today.
Date literals start at midnight in the user's locale, not at now minus a number of hours.
Using = with a date literal on a DateTime field matches the whole range; that is normal.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: Date Formats and Date Literals in WHERE

questions.q: A reusable selector builds this query at run time. It fails with 'Variable does not exist: `acct.Id`'. Which two changes fix it? (Choose 2)
options: Assign the value to a local variable first (`Id acctId = acct.Id;`) and bind `:acctId` in the string
Concatenate the sObject into the string: '... WHERE AccountId = \'' + acct + '\''
Use `Database.queryWithBinds` with `':acctId'` in the string and a Map such as `{'acctId' => acct.Id}`
Declare the `acct` parameter as `final` so `Database.query` can see its fields
Change the bind to `:acct.get('Id')`
questions.explain: `Database.query` only binds simple variables, not fields like `acct.Id`. Copy the value into a local variable first. Or pass it in the bind map of `Database.queryWithBinds`.
wrong: It pastes the whole sObject as text, not its Id, and opens the door to SOQL injection.
`final` doesn't change how bind variables are found.
Method calls aren't supported in bind expressions in dynamic SOQL.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Dynamic SOQL

questions.q: A pipeline filter builds its bind map from user choices. A bug adds a second key. What happens when this runs?
options: It returns Qualification Opportunities, because the last value put wins
It returns Prospecting Opportunities, because the key `'stage'` matches the bind name exactly
A `QueryException` is thrown, because the bind map has keys that differ only in case
It doesn't compile, because `Map<String, Object>` can't hold an Integer value
questions.explain: `queryWithBinds` matches key names without caring about case. Keys that differ only in case clash, so it throws a `QueryException`.
wrong: Both keys stay in the map, since String keys care about case, so no 'last one wins'.
Bind names match without caring about case, so both keys match and clash.
`Map<String, Object>` holds any value type, including Integer.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Dynamic SOQL

questions.q: A generic export utility reads values from queried records by field path. What happens on the last line, and what is the fix?
options: It throws an `SObjectException` (invalid field); read the parent first: `rec.getSObject('Account').get('Name')`
It returns the Account name, because `get()` follows relationship paths
It returns null, because parent fields must be read with `get('Account__r.Name')`
It throws a `TypeException` on the cast; use `String.valueOf(rec.get('Account.Name'))`
questions.explain: `get()` only reads fields on the record itself, not dot paths. Use `getSObject('Account')` to reach the parent, then `get('Name')` on it.
wrong: `get()` doesn't follow dot paths.
Account is a standard lookup named Account, and `get()` still can't follow paths.
The error is the bad field name, not the cast.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Dynamic DML

questions.q: A generic CSV export receives an object name and a list of field names from a Lightning page. It must keep only the fields that exist and that the running user can read. What goes in the if condition?
options: `tok.getDescribe().isUpdateable()`
`fieldMap.containsKey(f)`
`tok != null && tok.getDescribe().isPermissionable()`
`tok != null && tok.getDescribe().isAccessible()`
questions.explain: First make sure the field exists, then ask if the user can read it. Check `tok != null`, then `DescribeFieldResult.isAccessible()`.
wrong: `isUpdateable()` checks edit access, which would drop read-only fields, and it fails on a null token.
`containsKey` only proves the field exists, not that the user can read it.
`isPermissionable()` says if permissions can be set on the field, not whether this user has them.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Understanding Apex Describe Information

questions.q: Tax rules differ by region, so the org stores each region's handler class name in Custom Metadata (for example, `'EmeaTaxHandler'`). Every handler implements the `TaxHandler` interface. Which line creates the right handler at run time?
options: `TaxHandler h = new Type(cfg.Handler_Class__c);`
`TaxHandler h = (TaxHandler) Type.forName(cfg.Handler_Class__c).newInstance();`
`TaxHandler h = (TaxHandler) Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(cfg.Handler_Class__c).newSObject();`
`TaxHandler h = Type.forName(cfg.Handler_Class__c);`
questions.explain: To build a class from its name, first find its type, then make an object. `Type.forName` gives the `System.Type`, `newInstance()` creates the object, and the cast lets you call the interface.
wrong: `Type` has no public constructor that takes a class name.
`getGlobalDescribe()` describes sObjects, not Apex classes.
`Type.forName` returns a `Type`, not an object; you still need `newInstance()` and a cast.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Type Class

questions.q: A validation rule on Opportunity blocks saving when `Discount__c` > 30 and `Approved__c` is false. A before update trigger raises the discount for Strategic accounts. A rep edits the Next Step on a Strategic Opportunity (`Approved__c` is false) in the UI. What happens?
options: The save succeeds, because validation rules run before `before update` triggers and only see the rep's input
The save succeeds, because validation rules don't evaluate field values set by Apex
It's blocked: custom validation rules run after before triggers, so they see `Discount__c = 35`
The save succeeds, and the validation rule blocks the record later when a workflow rule re-runs validation
questions.explain: Custom validation rules run after before triggers. So the rule sees the `Discount__c` of 35 that the trigger set, and it blocks the save.
wrong: Custom validation rules run after before triggers, not before them.
Validation rules check the final values, including ones set by before triggers.
Custom validation rules don't run again after workflow field updates, and the save is already blocked.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: `Touches__c` on a Lead is 1. A user changes it to 10. A workflow rule field update then adds 1, making it 11. The after update trigger below runs again after the workflow field update. What does that second run log?
options: old=1 new=11
old=10 new=11
old=11 new=11
old=1 new=10
questions.explain: This is a known quirk. In the trigger re-run after a workflow field update, `Trigger.old` still holds the value from before the first update. So old is 1, not the 10 the user saved.
wrong: That's the documented quirk: `Trigger.old` isn't the value from just before the workflow update.
`Trigger.old` never holds the workflow's new value.
`Trigger.new` in the re-run includes the workflow field update (11).
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: An org still has a legacy workflow rule with a field update on Case. When it fires during an update, which two things run again for that record? (Choose 2)
options: Custom validation rules
Before update and after update triggers (one more time)
Duplicate rules
System validations
Before-save record-triggered flows
questions.explain: A workflow field update saves the record again, but only part of the line runs twice. System validations and the before and after update triggers run once more. Custom validation rules, flows, duplicate rules, processes and escalation rules do not.
wrong: Custom validation rules don't run again after a workflow field update.
Duplicate rules don't run again.
Flows don't run again for a workflow field update.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: An admin adds an after-save record-triggered flow on Opportunity that updates the triggering record's `Next_Review__c` field. Since then, reps get two follow-up Tasks when they move a deal to Negotiation. What is happening, and what is the best fix?
options: Record-triggered flows always run in a separate transaction, so the trigger fires once in each; make the flow run asynchronously
The platform always fires after update triggers twice when any flow exists on the object; use a `static Boolean` to stop the second run
Duplicate rules re-run after the flow and copy the Task; turn off the duplicate rule on Task
The flow's update re-runs the save, so the trigger fires twice; create the Task only if `StageName` changed vs `Trigger.oldMap`
questions.explain: When an after-save flow updates the record, the record is saved again, and update triggers fire again. In that second save, the old stage is already Negotiation. Comparing to `Trigger.oldMap` stops the extra Task.
wrong: The flow runs in the same transaction as the save that started it.
The flow's DML fires the triggers again, not just having a flow; and a `static Boolean` skips later 200-record chunks.
Duplicate rules don't create records.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: `Invoice_Line__c` is the detail in a master-detail with `Invoice__c`, which has a roll-up summary field `Total__c`. `Invoice__c` has an after update trigger that queues an ERP sync. A Data Loader job inserts 500 lines spread across 20 Invoices. What happens to the Invoice trigger?
options: It doesn't fire, because roll-up summaries are calculated after commit
It fires for the 20 Invoices, because recalculating the roll-up summary sends each parent through the save procedure
It doesn't fire, because roll-up summary fields update like formula fields, without a save
It fires only if the Data Loader job uses all-or-none mode
questions.explain: A roll-up summary saves the parent record. When a child changes the roll-up, the parent goes through the save line, so its update triggers fire. Check that `Total__c` really changed before queueing work.
wrong: Roll-ups are recalculated before commit, in the same transaction.
Roll-up summaries are stored values; the parent is saved and its triggers fire.
All-or-none mode doesn't decide whether parent triggers fire.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: On Lead, a before-save flow sets Rating, a before insert trigger lowercases Email, a duplicate rule blocks Leads with a matching Email, and an after insert trigger creates a Task. Which two statements are true for a new Lead? (Choose 2)
options: If the duplicate rule blocks the Lead, the after insert trigger still runs but its Task is rolled back
The duplicate rule runs before custom validation rules
The before insert trigger can only see the Rating value after the Lead is committed
The before-save flow runs before the before insert trigger
The duplicate rule checks the lowercased Email set by the trigger
questions.explain: The line is: before-save flows, before triggers, validation, then duplicate rules, then save. So the duplicate rule sees the email the trigger lowercased. If it blocks, after triggers never run.
wrong: When a duplicate rule blocks, no later steps run, including after triggers.
Duplicate rules run after custom validation rules.
The before-save flow already ran, so the trigger sees Rating in `Trigger.new`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: An integration calls `Database.update(accounts, false)` on 100 Accounts. Two fail a validation rule. The after update trigger below writes audit rows and uses a `static Set` to stop recursion. What is the outcome?
options: 98 Accounts are saved with 98 audit rows
98 Accounts are saved with 196 audit rows, because the trigger ran twice
98 Accounts are saved, but no audit rows are saved
The whole update fails with 'Too many batch retries in the presence of Apex triggers and partial failures'
questions.explain: With partial success, Salesforce rolls back the first try and re-runs the trigger on the 98 good records. Static variables aren't reset, so the Set already holds their Ids. The retry skips them, and the first try's audit rows were rolled back.
wrong: The retry skips every record, because the `static Set` wasn't reset.
The first try's audit rows are rolled back, and the retry inserts none.
That error happens only if records still fail on the third try.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk DML Exception Handling; Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: This trigger stamps the date when the stage changes. Updates work, but every new Opportunity fails. Why?
options: `Trigger.oldMap` is null on insert, so `oldMap.get()` throws a `NullPointerException`; check `Trigger.isUpdate`
A null old record makes the comparison true, so the stamp is set on every insert
The trigger doesn't compile, because `Trigger.oldMap` can't be used in a trigger that also handles before insert
`o.Id` is null in before insert, so the loop skips the record and a required field stays blank
questions.explain: Insert triggers have no old records. `Trigger.old` and `Trigger.oldMap` exist only in update and delete triggers. Calling `get()` on the null map throws a `NullPointerException`, so check `Trigger.isUpdate` first.
wrong: The code never gets that far: `get()` on a null map throws first.
It compiles; the error happens at run time on insert.
The loop still runs; the failure is the null oldMap.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Trigger Context Variables

questions.q: A sign-up form batch inserts 50 Contacts with `Database.insert(contacts, false)`. Four have '@`test.invalid`' emails. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: The `SaveResult` for each blocked Contact has `isSuccess() = false` and the message 'Use a real email address.'
The 46 valid Contacts are saved
`Database.insert` throws a `DmlException` after the first blocked Contact
All 50 Contacts roll back, because `addError` in a trigger fails the whole DML call
The 4 blocked Contacts are saved with Email cleared
questions.explain: `addError` fails only the records it marks. With `allOrNone = false`, the 46 good Contacts save. Each of the 4 failures shows up in its `SaveResult` with the message.
wrong: With `allOrNone = false`, errors come back in `SaveResults`, not as an exception.
Only the records marked with `addError` fail when partial success is allowed.
Records with `addError` aren't saved at all.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk DML Exception Handling; Trigger Context Variables

questions.q: An Apex REST endpoint inserts 150 Cases in one `insert` statement. What happens with this trigger?
options: It uses 1 SOQL query, because the platform combines identical `SELECT` queries in a loop
It succeeds, because Apex REST requests get the asynchronous limit of 200 queries
It succeeds, but Tasks are created only for the first 100 Cases
The insert fails with a `LimitException` on the 101st query, and none of the 150 Cases are saved
questions.explain: The query runs once per Case, so the 101st query breaks the synchronous limit of 100. A `LimitException` can't be caught, so the whole transaction rolls back. None of the 150 Cases save.
wrong: Apex doesn't merge queries; each pass through the loop runs one.
Apex REST runs with synchronous limits.
A limit exception rolls back everything; nothing is partly saved.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: This onboarding code retries after a failed Contact insert. What happens at the second insert of `a`?
options: It inserts the Account named 'Globex (retry)'
It fails: `a` still holds the Id from the rolled-back insert; clone it without the Id first
`Database.rollback(sp)` throws an exception, because the savepoint was set before the Account insert
It creates a second Account, so the org ends with two Globex records
questions.explain: A rollback undoes the database work, not your variables. The Account variable still holds its Id, so inserting it again fails. Clone it without the Id first.
wrong: The variable still has an Id, so the insert fails.
Rolling back to an earlier savepoint is the normal use.
The first insert was rolled back and the second fails, so no Account remains.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: `Importer.run()` is called once with 150 Leads in a new transaction. Afterwards, how many DML statements have been used, and what is `Importer.attempts`?
options: 1 DML statement; `attempts = 0`
1 DML statement; `attempts = 1`
3 DML statements; `attempts = 1`
3 DML statements; `attempts = 0`
questions.explain: Savepoints cost DML too. `setSavepoint()`, `insert` and `rollback()` each count as a DML statement, so 3 in total. A rollback doesn't undo static variables, so `attempts` stays 1.
wrong: Savepoints and rollbacks count as DML statements, and static variables aren't rolled back.
`setSavepoint()` and `rollback()` also count as DML statements.
Static variables keep their values after a rollback.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: In API version 62.0, this method rolls back a failed order and then sends a failure notice to the ERP with an HTTP callout. The callout throws a `CalloutException`. What should the developer change?
options: Call `Database.releaseSavepoint(sp)` after the rollback and before the callout
Nothing; rolling back removes the pending DML, so the callout should work, and the error means the endpoint is down
Call `Database.setSavepoint()` again after the rollback, so the callout runs after a fresh savepoint
Call `Database.releaseSavepoint(sp)` before `Database.rollback(sp)`
questions.explain: Since API 60.0, every active savepoint must be released before a callout. Call `Database.releaseSavepoint(sp)` after the rollback and before the callout. Otherwise it fails with 'All active Savepoints must be released before making callouts'.
wrong: An active savepoint still blocks the callout, even with no pending DML.
A new savepoint is one more active savepoint, which blocks the callout too.
Rolling back after a release throws an error, and the insert would still be pending.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: A data import logs failures to `Import_Error__c`. Support says the `Record_Id__c` column is always blank, so they can't tell which source rows failed. What is the bug and the fix?
options: `getErrors()` is empty for failed records; call `getMessage()` on the `SaveResult` directly
`SaveResults` come back in random order; sort them by Id before logging
`Database.insert(rows, false)` throws on the first failure, so the loop only logs successes
`getId()` is null for failed rows; loop by index and use `rows[i]` (e.g. its external key)
questions.explain: A failed row never got an Id, so `getId()` is null. `SaveResults` come back in the same order as the input list. Loop by index and log `rows[i]` instead.
wrong: Failed `SaveResults` do hold their errors in `getErrors()`.
Results come in the same order as the input list, which is why the index works.
With `allOrNone = false`, failures are returned, not thrown.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: SaveResult Class

questions.q: A Queueable syncs Account names to a marketing tool. It is enqueued from a button. What happens when the job runs?
options: It sends the names that were cached when the job was enqueued
It throws a `NullPointerException`: `transient` members aren't serialized, so `cache` is null
It doesn't compile, because the `transient` keyword isn't allowed in classes that implement Queueable
It sends the names, but they may be stale because the cache isn't refreshed
questions.explain: A Queueable is saved (serialized) when it's enqueued. Transient variables are skipped and come back null. So `cache.get(i)` throws a `NullPointerException` in `execute()`.
wrong: Transient variables aren't serialized, so the cache is gone.
`transient` compiles fine; it just isn't serialized.
The cache is null, not stale.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex

questions.q: A batch job runs with the default scope of 200. For each record it enqueues a Queueable to call a partner API. What happens in the first `execute()`?
options: 200 Queueable jobs are queued and run in parallel
Up to 50 jobs are queued, then a `LimitException` is thrown
The second `enqueueJob` call throws a `LimitException`; async code can add only one Queueable
All 200 jobs are queued but held in the flex queue until the batch's `finish()` method completes
questions.explain: Batch `execute()` is asynchronous, and async code can enqueue only one Queueable. The second `enqueueJob` call throws a `LimitException`. Collect the Ids and enqueue one job for the whole chunk.
wrong: Only one job can be enqueued from an asynchronous transaction.
50 is the synchronous limit, but batch `execute()` is asynchronous.
Enqueued jobs aren't held for `finish()`, and the second enqueue fails anyway.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: An order page enqueues an ERP sync with these options. A user clicks Sync twice, in two separate transactions, while the first job is still waiting in the queue. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: Both jobs run, with the second starting 2 minutes after the first
In an Apex test, `Test.stopTest()` waits 2 real minutes before running the job
The second enqueue throws a `DuplicateMessageException`
The job waits at least 2 minutes before it can start
The signature uses only the class name, so `orderId` is ignored
questions.explain: A duplicate signature blocks a matching job that is already queued. The second enqueue throws a `DuplicateMessageException`. `MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes` makes the job wait 0-10 minutes, but tests ignore the delay.
wrong: A duplicate signature stops the second job from being enqueued at all.
The delay is ignored in Apex tests.
The signature is built from what you add: here the order Id and a string.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex; Apex Reference Guide: QueueableDuplicateSignature.Builder Class

questions.q: This Queueable hits the CPU time limit after processing 120 rows. What does the `Job_Log__c` record show?
options: `Count__c = 120` and `Result__c = 'UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION'`
`Count__c = 0`, because the finalizer's state is captured when it is attached
No log is created, because a limit exception also stops the finalizer
`Count__c = 120` and `Result__c = 'SUCCESS'`, because the finalizer handles the exception
questions.explain: The finalizer sees its own variables as they are when the job ends. So `processed` is 120. It runs in its own transaction, so its insert commits even though the job's DML rolls back.
wrong: You can change a finalizer after attaching it; its state at the end of the job is used.
The finalizer runs in its own transaction, even after an uncatchable limit exception.
`getResult()` reports `UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`; the finalizer doesn't change the job's result.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: A team is adding a Transaction Finalizer to a Queueable that posts invoices. Which two statements about finalizers are true? (Choose 2)
options: A finalizer can enqueue one asynchronous job (Queueable, future or batch)
The finalizer runs in the same transaction as the Queueable, so it can roll back the Queueable's DML
Calling `System.attachFinalizer` twice attaches two finalizers that both run
Each finalizer run counts as an extra execution against the daily async Apex limit
A finalizer can make callouts
questions.explain: A finalizer runs in its own transaction after the Queueable, so it can't undo the job's DML. Inside it you may make callouts and enqueue one async job (Queueable, future or batch). Only one finalizer is allowed per job, and it doesn't count against the daily async limit.
wrong: The Queueable and its finalizer run in separate transactions.
Only one finalizer can be attached to a Queueable job.
A finalizer doesn't count as an extra async execution.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: This batch runs over 1,000 records with a scope of 200. Each chunk has 3 failed deletes. What does `finish()` log?
questions.explain: `Database.Stateful` keeps instance variables between chunks, so `processed` reaches 1,000. Static variables aren't kept between batch transactions, so `errors` is 0 again in `finish()`.
wrong: Static variables reset in each batch transaction, even with `Database.Stateful`.
`Database.Stateful` keeps the instance variable across all 5 chunks.
The instance variable is kept because the class implements `Database.Stateful`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Use Batch Apex

questions.q: A batch's `start()` returns a `QueryLocator` that finds 9,000 records. It is started with the line below. How many times does `execute()` run?
questions.code: Id jobId = Database.executeBatch(new ArchiveOrdersBatch(), 5000);
options: None: a `LimitException` is thrown because the scope is above 2,000
questions.explain: A `QueryLocator` scope can be at most 2,000. A bigger number is cut down, not rejected. So 9,000 records run as four chunks of 2,000 and one of 1,000: 5 runs.
wrong: A scope above 2,000 isn't used as given with a `QueryLocator`.
45 would fit the default scope of 200, but a scope was passed.
No error is thrown; Salesforce splits the records into chunks of up to 2,000.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Use Batch Apex

questions.q: This batch marks Shipments as sent and posts each one to a carrier API. Every `execute()` fails with 'You have uncommitted work pending'. What is the fix?
options: Add `Database.AllowsCallouts` to the class definition
Call an `@future(callout=true)` method for each record from `execute()`
Make all the callouts first, then run the update on the scope at the end of `execute()`
Raise the scope to 2,000 so fewer transactions make callouts
questions.explain: A callout can't come after unsaved DML in the same transaction. Make all the callouts first, then run the update at the end of `execute()`. Each `execute()` is its own transaction.
wrong: The class already implements `Database.AllowsCallouts`; the problem is the order.
Future methods can't be called from Batch Apex.
A bigger scope doesn't fix the order, and 2,000 callouts would pass the limit of 100.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Callout Limits and Limitations; Use Batch Apex

questions.q: This scheduled class runs nightly, but the callout fails. Which two changes let the nightly price sync reach the ERP? (Choose 2)
options: Add `Database.AllowsCallouts` to the Schedulable class
From `execute()`, enqueue a Queueable that implements `Database.AllowsCallouts` and makes the callout
From `execute()`, call a `static` `@future(callout=true)` method that makes the callout
Wrap `http.send()` in try/catch to handle the `CalloutException`
Return a Continuation from `execute()`
questions.explain: Scheduled Apex can't make synchronous callouts, and adding `Database.AllowsCallouts` to a Schedulable does nothing. Move the callout into async code that allows it: a Queueable with `Database.AllowsCallouts`, or a `@future(callout=true)` method. A Schedulable's `execute()` may call either.
wrong: `Database.AllowsCallouts` works for Queueable and Batch Apex, not a Schedulable class.
Catching the exception doesn't make the callout work.
Continuations are for Lightning and Visualforce controllers, not scheduled jobs.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex Scheduler

questions.q: A nightly batch sometimes fails a chunk with an uncatchable limit exception. Operations needs the Ids of the records in each failed chunk saved, so they can be retried the next night. What should the developer do?
options: Implement `Database.RaisesPlatformEvents` and save `JobScope` Ids from a `BatchApexErrorEvent` trigger
Wrap the `execute()` body in try/catch for `LimitException` and save the scope Ids in the catch block
Implement `Database.Stateful`, add failed Ids to a list in `execute()`, and save them in `finish()`
Attach a Transaction Finalizer in `execute()` to save the Ids of the chunk if it fails
questions.explain: A dying chunk can't save anything itself, so let the platform report it. With `Database.RaisesPlatformEvents`, an unhandled batch error publishes a `BatchApexErrorEvent`. Its `JobScope` field holds the failed record Ids.
wrong: Limit exceptions can't be caught.
The failing chunk dies before it can record anything, so its change is lost.
Transaction Finalizers only work with Queueable jobs.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Use Batch Apex

questions.q: `Order_Placed__e` is set to Publish After Commit. `Audit_Log__e` is set to Publish Immediately. `chargeCard()` throws an exception that nothing catches. What reaches subscribers?
options: Both events, because `EventBus.publish` isn't affected by rollbacks
Neither event, because events are always discarded when the transaction fails
Only the `Order_Placed__e` event, because it was published first
Only the `Audit_Log__e` event; the Order and the `Order_Placed__e` event are both rolled back
questions.explain: Publish Immediately events go out the moment you publish, even if the transaction fails later. Publish After Commit events go out only if it commits. Here it fails, so only `Audit_Log__e` is sent.
wrong: Publish After Commit events are dropped when the transaction fails.
Publish Immediately events are sent no matter what happens to the transaction.
Publish order doesn't matter; the transaction failed, so the after-commit event is never sent.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Platform Event Fields; Publish Event Messages with Apex

questions.q: A developer marks a record as 'Sent' when the publish result is successful. A reviewer says `isSuccess()` doesn't mean what the developer thinks. What does it mean, and how can the code learn the final result?
options: All subscribers received and processed the event; no further check is needed
Only that the publish was queued; pass an `EventPublishFailureCallback` or `SuccessCallback` to learn the result
The subscriber trigger finished without errors; query `EventBusSubscriber` to confirm
The event was committed with the transaction; check `Limits.getDMLStatements()` afterwards to confirm the final result
questions.explain: Publishing is asynchronous. A successful `SaveResult` only means the publish was queued. The final result arrives in a publish callback, like `EventPublishFailureCallback`.
wrong: `isSuccess()` says nothing about delivery or processing by subscribers.
This result can't tell the publisher when a subscriber trigger finishes.
A DML counter can't show whether an event was published.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Publish Event Messages with Apex; Get the Result of Asynchronous Platform Event Publishing with Apex Publish Callbacks

questions.q: This platform event trigger receives a batch of 1,000 events. Event number 301 has a bad value, and the trigger throws an uncaught exception there. The trigger doesn't use `setResumeCheckpoint` or `RetryableException`. What happens?
options: All logs are rolled back, and the whole batch is retried automatically up to 9 times
The logs for the first 300 events stay committed, and the trigger fires again starting at event 301
Logs for the first 300 stay committed; the rest of the batch isn't processed by this trigger
All logs are rolled back, and the trigger moves straight to the error state
questions.explain: After an uncaught exception, the trigger stops and skips the rest of the batch. DML done before the exception stays committed. Use `setResumeCheckpoint` to pick up after the last good event.
wrong: Automatic retries happen only when the trigger throws `EventBus.RetryableException`.
Resuming at the next event needs `setResumeCheckpoint`.
DML isn't rolled back for an uncaught exception, and the error state comes from too many retries.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Subscribe to Platform Event Notifications with Apex Triggers

questions.q: Payment events sometimes arrive before the ERP has created the matching `Invoice__c` records, so the trigger below retries. Which two statements about this trigger are true? (Choose 2)
options: When `RetryableException` is thrown, DML done earlier in that trigger run is rolled back
Only the events after the one that failed are sent again
Without the `retries` check, the platform would keep retrying forever
On retry, every event in the batch is sent again, in the original `ReplayId` order
Retried batches always have exactly the same events and size as the first one
questions.explain: Throwing `EventBus.RetryableException` undoes the trigger's DML and resends the whole batch in `ReplayId` order. The trigger can be retried 9 times, then it moves to the error state.
wrong: That's how `setResumeCheckpoint` works; a retry resends the whole batch.
After 9 retries the trigger moves to the error state and stops.
Resent batches can be bigger, because new events can join them.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Retry Event Triggers with EventBus.RetryableException

questions.q: When an Opportunity is Closed Won, a legacy middleware must receive the Opportunity Id and Amount. It can only accept SOAP messages pushed to its HTTPS endpoint, it is sometimes down for a few hours, and the admin wants no Apex. What should the team use?
options: An outbound message action that sends the fields to the middleware endpoint
Change Data Capture on Opportunity, with the middleware subscribing to the change channel
A custom platform event published by a flow, with an Apex trigger that makes the callout
An Apex REST service that the middleware calls every hour
questions.explain: The middleware only takes pushed SOAP, and no Apex is allowed. An outbound message pushes a SOAP message with chosen fields to an endpoint. It needs no code and retries while the endpoint is down.
wrong: CDC needs the middleware to subscribe as a client; it doesn't push SOAP to an endpoint.
This needs Apex, and platform event triggers generally can't make callouts directly.
That needs Apex and polling, and the middleware can only receive pushed messages.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Outbound Messaging; Change Data Capture Developer Guide

questions.q: A shipping partner's API returns HTTP 503 with an HTML maintenance page during upgrades. What happens in this code?
options: `Http.send()` throws a `CalloutException` for the 503 status, so the catch block sets `Sync_Status__c` to Failed
`Http.send()` returns null for a 503, so `res.getBody()` throws a `NullPointerException`
The platform retries the callout up to 3 times before returning the 503
`send()` returns normally, then parsing HTML throws an uncaught `JSONException`; check `getStatusCode()` first
questions.explain: HTTP error codes don't throw in Apex. `send()` returns the 503 response normally, and parsing the HTML throws an uncaught `JSONException`. Check `getStatusCode()` before you parse the body.
wrong: `CalloutException` covers things like timeouts and failed connections, not HTTP error codes.
`send()` returns an `HttpResponse` for any HTTP status.
Apex doesn't retry callouts automatically.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: HTTP Classes; Apex Reference Guide: HttpResponse Class

questions.q: A Lightning controller logs an audit entry asynchronously and then calls a credit check service. No DML runs in the method. The callout throws an exception. Why?
options: Future methods run before the rest of the method, so the audit DML is pending when the callout runs
Queuing a future method is pending work, so the callout fails ('uncommitted work pending'); call out first
A controller can't make a callout and queue async work in the same request; split them into two Lightning calls
A future method and a callout in one transaction exceed the callout limit
questions.explain: Queuing async work counts as pending work, just like DML. Pending work includes DML, queued async Apex like future methods, scheduled Apex and sending email. Make the callout before any of them.
wrong: Future methods run after the transaction commits, not before the callout.
Both are allowed in one request if the callout comes first.
One callout is far below the limit of 100; this is about order.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Callout Limits and Limitations

questions.q: A method calls two endpoints: a token service, then a quotes service. The test below fails because both callouts get the same JSON. Which two changes give each callout its own fake response? (Choose 2)
options: Call `Test.setMock` twice, once for each endpoint
Use `MultiStaticResourceCalloutMock` and map each endpoint to its own static resource
Use `Test.setMock(WebServiceMock.class, ...)` for the second endpoint
Add `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)` so the second callout, to the quotes service, reaches the real endpoint
Write an `HttpCalloutMock` class whose `respond()` method returns a different response based on `req.getEndpoint()`
questions.explain: Each callout needs its own fake answer. `MultiStaticResourceCalloutMock` maps each endpoint to a static resource. A custom `HttpCalloutMock` can also check `req.getEndpoint()` and answer differently.
wrong: The last setMock call replaces the earlier one; it doesn't map mocks to endpoints.
`WebServiceMock` is for WSDL-based SOAP callouts, not `HttpRequest`.
Tests can't make real callouts, whatever SeeAllData says.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Testing HTTP Callouts Using Static Resources; Testing HTTP Callouts by Implementing the HttpCalloutMock Interface

questions.q: A partner POSTs JSON orders to `/services/apexrest/orders`. The contract says: 201 with a JSON body on success, and 422 with a JSON error message when validation fails. Which design meets it?
options: A `global static String` `@HttpPost` method that returns `'201'` or `'422'` as its result
An `@HttpPost` method that throws a custom exception for validation failures, so the platform answers with 422
A `global static void` `@HttpPost` method that parses `requestBody` and sets `RestContext.response` `statusCode` and `responseBody`
A `global static Id` `@HttpPost` method that inserts the order and returns its new Id, so the platform answers with 201 Created
questions.explain: To choose the status code and body, set them yourself on `RestContext.response`. With no parameters, the raw request body is in `RestContext.request.requestBody`.
wrong: The returned string becomes the body, and the status stays 200.
An unhandled exception returns 400 or 500, never 422.
The platform doesn't switch to 201 for you; you set the status code yourself.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex REST Methods

questions.q: A developer writes this Apex REST resource for a mobile app. It doesn't compile. Which two problems must be fixed? (Choose 2)
options: `urlMapping` must include the full path, starting with `/services/apexrest`, for example `'/services/apexrest/accounts/*'`
Apex REST methods can't return `List<Account>`
A class can't have two methods annotated with the same HTTP method (`@HttpGet`)
A `@RestResource` class can't be declared `with sharing`
`@HttpGet` methods can't have parameters; read the name from `RestContext.request.params` instead
questions.explain: A `@RestResource` class allows only one method per HTTP verb. Also, GET and DELETE methods take no parameters, because those requests have no body.
wrong: `urlMapping` is relative to `/services/apexrest`, so you don't add that prefix.
Lists of sObjects are allowed return types.
`with sharing` is allowed and common on REST resources.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex REST Methods

questions.q: A web form posts this JSON to the Apex REST method below: `{"email": "ana@example.com", "source": "web"}`. The request fails. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: The JSON must wrap the object in a key named after the parameter: `{"customer": {...}}`
`CustomerDto` must implement `Serializable` to be used as a parameter
Even with the wrapper, `source` is null, because `transient` members aren't deserialized
The keys in the JSON must appear in the same order as the class's members
Only `global` members are deserialized from JSON, so a `public` or `private` member would always stay null
questions.explain: Apex REST matches top-level JSON keys to parameter names. So the body needs a `'customer'` key. Members marked `static` or `transient` aren't filled from the JSON.
wrong: Apex REST needs no `Serializable` interface.
Key names matter, but their order doesn't.
`Public`, `private` and `global` members are all filled from the JSON.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex REST Methods

questions.q: An insurance partner needs a SOAP API to file claims. This class doesn't compile. Which two members cause the errors? (Choose 2)
options: The `webservice` member variables in the inner `ClaimInput` class
The second `fileClaim` method, because `webservice` methods can't be overloaded
`fileClaim(ClaimInput)`, because `webservice` methods can't take user-defined types
`lookup()`, because `webservice` methods can't return a Map
The `global` keyword on the outer class, because `webservice` classes must be `public`
questions.explain: Apex won't allow two `webservice` methods with the same name. Maps, like Sets, can't be `webservice` parameters or return types.
wrong: `webservice` member variables in an inner class are how you expose a custom type.
Inner classes with `webservice` members can be used as parameters.
Classes with `webservice` methods must be `global`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Considerations for Using the webservice Keyword; Overloading Web Service Methods

questions.q: `Client__c` must show a live count of its Completed `Project__c` records. `Project__c` has a lookup (not master-detail) to `Client__c`, and it can't be converted because some Projects have no Client. Integrations mass-update Projects, and the count must stay right when a Project is deleted or restored from the Recycle Bin. What is the best solution?
options: An after insert, update, delete and undelete trigger on `Project__c` that recounts with one aggregate query
A roll-up summary field on `Client__c` that counts Completed Projects
A record-triggered flow on `Project__c` that runs when a record is created, updated or deleted and recounts the Client
A formula field on `Client__c` that counts the related Projects
questions.explain: Only an Apex trigger covers every case here. Roll-up summaries need master-detail, and record-triggered flows can't run on undelete. A bulkified trigger with one aggregate query handles it all.
wrong: Roll-up summary fields aren't available on a lookup relationship.
Record-triggered flows can't run on undelete, so restored Projects wouldn't count.
Formula fields can't count child records.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers; Salesforce Help: Roll-Up Summary Field; Salesforce Help: Record-Triggered Flows

questions.q: A record-triggered flow on Account calls this action to get a credit score. In bulk loads, some Accounts get another Account's score. What is wrong?
options: Invocable methods can't run SOQL; pass the scores in from the flow instead
The method must be `global` to run in bulk
The flow calls the action once per record, so the List always holds one Id and the bug must be elsewhere
Outputs must match the inputs in size and order; loop over `accountIds` and look each one up in a Map
questions.explain: Flow bundles interviews into one call, and output number i must belong to input number i. Skipping Accounts with no score shifts every later result. Loop over `accountIds` and look each one up in a Map.
wrong: Invocable methods can run SOQL; that's how they get the scores.
`public` is enough for an invocable method; `global` isn't needed.
Flow batches interviews and passes many Ids in one call.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableMethod Annotation

questions.q: The team wants at most 3 attempts while the ERP is down for a day. What actually happens?
options: It stops after exactly 3 attempts, because `attempts` counts every run of `SyncJob` in the org
The `static` resets in each new transaction, so it retries until the platform's 5-retry limit
It never retries at all, because a finalizer isn't allowed to enqueue the class it's attached to
It retries forever, since the finalizer's own transaction resets the retry counter too
questions.explain: The finalizer runs in its own transaction, so `SyncJob.attempts` is 0 there every time. The team's cap never kicks in. The platform stops the chain after 5 consecutive failed re-enqueues; pass the count through the constructor instead.
wrong: Statics reset in every transaction, so the finalizer always sees `attempts = 0`.
A finalizer can enqueue one async job, including a new copy of its own Queueable.
Re-enqueuing after consecutive failures is capped at 5, so it never retries forever.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: Inside the Queueable, the code attaches this finalizer as `f`, then adds 4 messages to `f.errors` and sets `f.processed` to 50 before the job ends. What does the log show?
options: `Count__c` is 0 and `Errors__c` is blank, because the finalizer's state is captured when it's attached
`Count__c` is 50 and `Errors__c` lists all 4 errors, because the whole finalizer object is kept
`Count__c` is 50 and `Errors__c` is blank, because `transient` fields don't persist into the finalizer
No `Job_Log__c` is created at all, because a finalizer isn't allowed to run DML of its own
questions.explain: The finalizer uses its state as it is at the end of the Queueable. But `transient` variables are skipped by serialization. So `processed` arrives as 50, and the error messages are lost.
wrong: The finalizer uses its state at the end of the Queueable, so `processed` is 50.
Transient variables are skipped by serialization, so the errors don't arrive.
Finalizers run in their own transaction and can run DML.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: Every night about 400,000 Product price updates must go to an ERP, and each record needs its own HTTP callout. Which design fits the limits?
options: A scheduled Batch Apex class with `Database.AllowsCallouts` and a scope of 100 or less
A Schedulable class that calls an `@future(callout=true)` method once for every Product
A single Queueable that loops over all 400,000 Products and makes every callout in one run
A record-triggered flow on Product that calls the ERP whenever a price changes
questions.explain: Each record needs a callout, and one transaction allows only 100. Batch Apex gives every `execute()` its own limit of 100 callouts. So a scope of 100 or less with `Database.AllowsCallouts` fits, and a Schedulable starts it nightly.
wrong: One transaction can make only 50 future calls, far short of 400,000.
One transaction allows only 100 callouts, and it can't process 400,000 rows.
That sends prices during the day as they change, not as a nightly sync.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A developer's first design uses `@future`. Which two requirements mean they should switch to Queueable Apex instead? (Choose 2)
options: The job must make an HTTP callout to an external REST service using a Named Credential
The job must receive a `List<Order__c>` holding unsaved, in-memory changes
The job must run only after the triggering transaction has committed to the database
The job must start a second job when it finishes, in a chain
The job must be started from inside an Apex trigger
questions.explain: Future methods take only primitives, and they can't call another future method. Queueable takes sObjects and can enqueue a follow-up job.
wrong: `@future(callout=true)` supports callouts too.
Both future and Queueable jobs run after the transaction commits.
Both can be started from a trigger.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Future Methods; Queueable Apex

questions.q: A mass update sets Priority to High on 50 Cases in one transaction, but only one Case gets an escalation. Why?
options: Mass updates don't publish change events; only the one Case edited in the UI produced one
A CDC trigger gets at most one event per transaction, so the other 49 events are dropped
`Priority` is null in the other events because it's an unchanged field, so only one matches
The changes were merged into one event whose `recordIds` holds all 50 Ids; loop over them
questions.explain: One change event can cover many records. When the same change hits several records of one object in a transaction, Salesforce may merge them. `recordIds` then lists every Id, so loop over all of them.
wrong: Change events are published for every committed change, bulk updates included.
Change event triggers get batches of up to 2,000 events; nothing limits them to one per transaction.
Priority changed on all 50 Cases, so it is filled in the event.
questions.source: Change Data Capture Developer Guide: ChangeEventHeader Fields

questions.q: A user changes only the Phone of an Account. The sync receives the new phone but a null Name, and the ERP blanks the account name. What should the developer know?
options: Name is null because the user who changed the Phone isn't allowed to read the Account Name
Unchanged fields are null in Apex change events; send only the fields in `changedFields`
Change events never include the Name field; it must always be queried separately
The trigger needs `Trigger.oldMap` to fill in fields that didn't change in this update
questions.explain: In Apex change events, fields that didn't change are null. So send only the fields in `changedFields`. `nulledFields` tells a real null apart from an unchanged field.
wrong: The field is null because it didn't change, not because of user access.
Name is included whenever it changes, like on create or a rename.
Change event triggers have no `Trigger.old` or `oldMap`.
questions.source: Change Data Capture Developer Guide: Change Event Triggers

questions.q: When a Case is closed, the team must email the customer a survey, create a follow-up Task, and stamp `Last_Case_Closed__c` on the parent Account. Admins will maintain it, and the logic is simple. What is the optimal solution?
options: A before-save record-triggered flow on Case that sends the email, creates the Task and updates the Account
An after insert and after update Apex trigger on Case that calls a handler class
An after-save record-triggered flow on Case with an entry condition on closed Cases
A new workflow rule on Case with an email alert, a task action and a cross-object field update
questions.explain: Simple logic that admins maintain belongs in Flow. An after-save record-triggered flow can send email, create related records and update other records. Apex adds nothing here.
wrong: Before-save flows can only update the triggering record; they can't send email or touch other records.
It works, but Apex isn't needed for simple logic admins should maintain.
New workflow rules can't be created any more; Salesforce points automation to Flow.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Record-Triggered Flows; Workflow Rules Retirement

questions.q: An after-save record-triggered flow on Opportunity calls an invocable Apex action that posts to an ERP REST API when a deal is Closed Won. On the run-immediately path the callout is blocked. What should the developer do?
options: Put the action on a Run Asynchronously path, which runs after the record is committed
Set `callout=true` on the `@InvocableMethod`; the flow then runs the call in the background
Change it to a before-save flow, which runs before any DML, so the callout is allowed
Wrap the HTTP call in a try/catch inside the action so the flow can carry on to the end
questions.explain: The run-immediately path runs inside the save, where callouts aren't allowed. The Run Asynchronously path runs after the record commits. So the action can make its callout there.
wrong: `callout=true` only tells Flow the action makes callouts; it doesn't move the call out of the transaction.
Before-save flows can't call Apex actions at all.
Catching the error doesn't let the callout go through.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Run Parts of a Record-Triggered Flow Asynchronously; Apex Developer Guide: InvocableMethod Annotation

questions.q: An after update trigger on Case sets a field on the same Cases and saves them again. In that second (recursive) save, which two run again for those Cases? (Choose 2)
options: Before update triggers on Case
Assignment rules that route the Case to a queue
After update triggers on Case, including this one
Auto-response rules that email the Case contact
Escalation rules for Case
questions.explain: A **recursive save** happens when code saves the same records again inside the first save. The DML fires the triggers again, so before and after update triggers run. Salesforce skips the steps from assignment rules through roll-up summaries.
