wrong: Assignment rules are one of the steps skipped in a recursive save.
Auto-response rules are skipped in a recursive save too.
Escalation rules fall inside the skipped steps as well.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: On Opportunity, a before-save flow sets `Stage_Gate__c` to 'Review'. A before update trigger then sets it to 'Ready' when `Score__c` > 80. A validation rule blocks 'Ready' when `Approver__c` is blank. A user saves a record with a score of 90 and no approver. What happens?
options: It saves as 'Review', because the before-save flow runs after the trigger and overwrites it
It saves as 'Ready', because validation rules run before triggers and saw 'Review'
The save is blocked: validation runs after the trigger and sees 'Ready'
It saves as 'Ready', because validation rules ignore values set by Apex code
questions.explain: Before-save flows run first, then before triggers, then custom validation rules. So the rule checks the value the trigger set: 'Ready'. With no approver, the save fails.
wrong: Before-save flows run before before triggers, not after them.
Custom validation rules run after before triggers.
Validation rules check the final values, whoever set them.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: An after insert trigger on `Order__c` calls `System.enqueueJob()` to notify the warehouse. Later in the same save, a roll-up summary updates the parent Account, and an Account validation rule fails. What happens to the warehouse job?
options: It never runs: the save rolls back, and the queued job goes with it
It runs, but its `execute()` fails because the `Order__c` record doesn't exist
It waits in the queue until a user fixes the Account and saves the Order again
It runs anyway, because an enqueued job is stored in the queue right away
questions.explain: Async jobs only start **after commit**. If the transaction rolls back, the Queueable jobs it queued are never processed. The failed Account validation rolls back the whole save, so the job never runs.
wrong: The job never starts, so it has no chance to fail on a missing record.
A rolled-back job is gone; a new save would enqueue a new one.
Jobs are held until commit, so a rollback cancels them.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex; Triggers and Order of Execution

questions.q: A data steward merges three duplicate Contacts into one. A developer's Contact triggers must log which records lost and which one won. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: A special `merge` trigger event fires once for the whole operation
In after delete, each losing record's `MasterRecordId` in `Trigger.old` holds the winner's Id
Cases and Opportunities moved to the winner fire their own update triggers
The winning record fires update triggers, like any normal update
`MasterRecordId` is already set in the before delete trigger
questions.explain: A merge has no trigger event of its own. Losing records fire delete triggers, and the winner fires update triggers. `MasterRecordId` points to the winner, but only in after delete.
wrong: There's no merge event; merges fire delete and update events.
Child records that get a new parent don't fire triggers.
`MasterRecordId` is only set in after delete events.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Triggers and Merge Statements

questions.q: To stamp `Last_Reviewed__c`, an after update trigger on Account queries the same Accounts, sets the field and calls `update`. Every edit now fails with 'Maximum trigger depth exceeded'. What is the best fix?
options: Call the `update` from an `@future` method so it runs outside the trigger
Use `Database.update(accts, false)` so that the repeated saves are allowed to finish
Wrap the `update` in a try/catch so the error is logged and the user's edit still saves
Set the field on `Trigger.new` in a before update trigger, with no DML
questions.explain: Each `update` on the same records fires the trigger again, which updates again, and so on. Apex stops this loop at a depth of 16. In a **before** trigger you just change `Trigger.new`, so no extra save happens.
wrong: The future update fires the trigger again, which then calls a future from a future and fails.
Partial success doesn't stop the trigger from firing again and again.
A try/catch hides the error but doesn't remove the loop.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Trigger Context Variable Considerations; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: Opportunity has two after-save record-triggered flows. 'Set Region' must always run before 'Notify Region Lead'. What should the admin do?
options: Move both flows to the Run Asynchronously path so that they run one at a time
Give 'Set Region' a lower Trigger Order value than 'Notify Region Lead'
Nothing: after-save flows always run in the order they were activated
Turn 'Set Region' into an Apex trigger, which always runs after flows
questions.explain: For record-triggered flows on the same object and timing, the **Trigger Order** value (1 to 2,000) decides which runs first. Lower numbers run first.
wrong: Async paths don't promise any order between flows.
Activation order isn't a promise; set a Trigger Order instead.
Apex after triggers run before after-save flows, not after them.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Manage Record-Triggered Flows (Flow Trigger Explorer)

questions.q: A web-to-lead import inserts 50 Leads in one transaction. How many of them get a `Score__c` from this trigger?
options: It doesn't compile, because a `Set<Id>` can't be used as a static guard
All 50, because each Lead gets added to the set the first time the loop sees it
Only the first Lead, because every new Lead has a null Id in before insert
None, because `Set.add()` returns false for a record that has no Id
questions.explain: In before insert, records have no Id yet, so `l.Id` is null. The first `add(null)` returns true, and every later one returns false. So only the first Lead is scored. Think: 50 kids all wearing the same blank name tag.
wrong: It compiles; the bug is the null Id, not the type.
All 50 share the same Id value: null.
A set can hold one null, so the first `add` returns true.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Trigger Context Variables; Apex Reference Guide: Set Class

questions.q: Every Contact insert fails with this trigger. Why?
options: `Trigger.newMap` is null in before insert, since new records have no Id
`Trigger.new` is read-only in before insert, so `Source__c` can't be set
`Trigger.newMap` can't be passed to another class; copy it into a new map first
Field changes in before insert must be saved with an `update` statement
questions.explain: `newMap` is keyed by record Id. In before insert, no Ids exist yet, so `Trigger.newMap` is null. Calling `keySet()` on it throws a `NullPointerException`.
wrong: Before triggers are exactly where you change `Trigger.new` fields.
Trigger maps can be passed to other methods like any map.
Changes in a before trigger are saved without any DML.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Trigger Context Variables

questions.q: Apex code runs `update opps;` on 50 Opportunities. A before update trigger calls `addError()` on 3 of them. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: The errors are shown only in the UI, so Apex can't catch them
The other 47 Opportunities are saved, and only the 3 flagged ones are skipped
No Opportunity is saved: one error rolls back the whole statement
`addError()` only takes effect in after triggers, so this whole update still succeeds
All 50 records are still checked, so the `DmlException` can list all 3 errors
questions.explain: An Apex DML statement is **all or nothing**. One `addError()` rolls back the whole `update`. Salesforce still checks every record, so the exception holds the full list of failures.
wrong: The errors come back to Apex as a `DmlException` you can catch.
Partial saves need `Database.update(opps, false)`, not a plain `update`.
`addError()` works in before and after triggers; before is faster.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Trigger Exceptions; Bulk DML Exception Handling

questions.q: This method runs in a synchronous transaction with 150 Account Ids. What happens?
options: The loop stops quietly after 100 queries, and the method returns normally
The catch block logs 'Too many SOQL queries: 101' and the finally block flushes
Only the finally block runs, because a `LimitException` skips catch blocks
The transaction stops with a `LimitException`; neither catch nor finally runs
questions.explain: Some errors can't be caught. A **`LimitException`** stops the transaction at once, and its catch and finally blocks don't run. The real fix is one query outside the loop.
wrong: Hitting a limit always throws; Apex never skips queries quietly.
`catch (Exception e)` can't catch a `LimitException`.
Uncatchable exceptions skip finally blocks too.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Exception Statements; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: An import uses a plain `insert rows;` on 300 records. Support wants a log line for each failed row: its position in the list and its error text. Which code in the `DmlException` catch block does this?
options: `log(e.getCause().getMessage());` inside a loop over every record in `rows`
`for (Integer i = 0; i < e.getNumDml(); i++) log(e.getDmlIndex(i), e.getDmlMessage(i));`
`log(e.getLineNumber(), e.getMessage());` once, since that one message already lists every failed row
`for (Database.SaveResult r : e.getResults()) log(r.getId(), r.getErrors());`
questions.explain: A `DmlException` keeps a list of every failed row. `getNumDml()` says how many failed. For each one, `getDmlIndex(i)` gives its position in the list and `getDmlMessage(i)` gives its error.
wrong: `getCause()` is for a wrapped exception and is usually null here.
`getLineNumber()` is the code line, and `getMessage()` names only the first error.
`DmlException` has no `getResults()`; save results come from `Database.insert(rows, false)`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Built-In Exceptions and Common Methods

questions.q: A data load inserts Contacts, several of them under the same Account. The load fails with this trigger. What is the cause and the fix?
options: An sObject built with just an Id can't be updated; query each Account first, then update
The update hits row locks on the Account; add `FOR UPDATE` to a query first
One list holds the same Account twice ('Duplicate id in list'); use a `Map<Id, Account>`
After insert triggers can't update parent records; move the logic to before insert
questions.explain: One DML list can't hold the same record Id twice, or it throws 'Duplicate id in list'. Two Contacts on one Account add that Account twice. A `Map<Id, Account>` keeps one entry per Id.
wrong: You can update a record with just its Id set; no query is needed.
Locks aren't the error here; the duplicate Ids are.
After triggers are the right place to update related records.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Bulk Apex Triggers; Common Bulk Trigger Idioms

questions.q: This job is enqueued from a button. What happens when `execute()` runs?
options: It throws a `NullPointerException`: `transient` fields are null when the job runs
It fails to enqueue, because an `HttpRequest` can't be a member of a Queueable
It runs, but `recordIds` is empty, because lists aren't kept between transactions
It works: the constructor's `HttpRequest` is kept with the job
questions.explain: When a Queueable is queued, its member variables are saved and restored when it runs. **`transient`** fields are skipped, so `template` is null in `execute()`. Build the request inside `execute()` instead.
wrong: As a `transient` field it isn't saved, so it can't block the enqueue.
Non-transient members like `recordIds` are kept, even lists and sObjects.
`transient` means 'don't save this', so the request is lost.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex

questions.q: A Queueable job runs in its own asynchronous transaction. Which two can its `execute()` method do? (Choose 2)
options: Enqueue one child Queueable job to continue the work
Make callouts without `Database.AllowsCallouts`, since it's already async
Enqueue two child Queueable jobs, one for each region
Call `@future` methods, up to 50 of them
Make 150 callouts, since async jobs get a higher callout limit
questions.explain: From a running Queueable you can add only **one** child job with `System.enqueueJob`. A Queueable may still call up to 50 future methods. Callouts need `Database.AllowsCallouts`, and the limit stays 100.
wrong: Queueables need `Database.AllowsCallouts` to make callouts.
Only one child job can be added from an executing job.
The callout limit is 100 in sync and async code alike.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A Queueable polls a partner for a report and re-enqueues itself until the report is ready. In production it must stop after at most 10 runs. Which approach is best?
options: Call `Limits.getQueueableJobs()` in each run and stop chaining once it reports 10 jobs
Nothing extra: chained Queueables stop at a stack depth of 5 in every kind of org
Keep a `static Integer` counter on the class, add 1 in each `execute()`, and stop when it reaches 10
Use `AsyncOptions` to set `MaximumQueueableStackDepth` to 10, and check `AsyncInfo` first
questions.explain: Each chained job is a new transaction, so static variables start over. `MaximumQueueableStackDepth` in `AsyncOptions` caps the chain. `AsyncInfo.getCurrentQueueableStackDepth()` tells the job how deep it is, so it can stop cleanly.
wrong: `Limits.getQueueableJobs()` counts only the jobs queued in this transaction.
The default depth of 5 applies only to Developer and Trial Edition orgs.
Static variables reset in every new job, so the counter never passes 1.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex (Adding a Queueable Job with a Specified Stack Depth)

questions.q: A trigger must hand Account Ids to an asynchronous method that calls a tax API. Which `@future` declaration compiles?
options: `@future(callout=true) public static void sync(List<Account> accounts)`
`@future(callout=true) public static void sync(Set<Id> accountIds)`
`@future(callout=true) public static Boolean sync(Set<Id> accountIds)`
`@future(callout=true) public void sync(Set<Id> accountIds)`
questions.explain: A future method must be `static` and return `void`. Its parameters must be primitives or collections of primitives, such as `Set<Id>`. sObjects can't be passed.
wrong: Future methods can't take sObjects; pass their Ids.
Future methods can only return `void`.
Future methods must be `static`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Future Annotation

questions.q: This works when users create Orders one at a time. A data load inserts 200 Orders in one chunk. What happens?
options: The first 50 jobs are queued and the other 150 are dropped without an error
Salesforce merges the 200 calls into one job, because `OrderSyncJob` is the same class
The 51st `enqueueJob` call throws a `LimitException`, and the whole chunk fails
All 200 jobs are queued, and each `execute()` runs in parallel as resources allow
questions.explain: A synchronous transaction can add at most **50** jobs with `System.enqueueJob`. The 51st call throws an uncatchable `LimitException`. Enqueue one job that takes all the Ids instead.
wrong: Going over a limit throws; nothing is dropped quietly.
Each call makes its own job; Salesforce never merges them.
The limit is 50 per transaction, so 200 calls can't all succeed.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: When an import Queueable fails, its finalizer builds a report that runs 120 SOQL queries. What happens in the finalizer?
options: It fails at query 101, because most finalizer limits are the synchronous ones
It shares the failed job's limits, so it can run only the queries the job didn't use
It runs fine, because finalizers aren't subject to governor limits
It runs fine, because finalizers get the async limit of 200 queries
questions.explain: A finalizer runs in its **own** transaction with fresh limits. Most are the synchronous limits, such as 100 SOQL queries. Only heap size and the async job counts use async limits.
wrong: The finalizer runs in a separate transaction with its own limits.
Finalizers have governor limits like any other Apex.
Finalizers use the synchronous SOQL limit of 100, not 200.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: A finalizer must post the error to a Slack webhook whenever its Queueable fails. Which statement is true?
options: `ctx.getException()` returns the last exception the job caught, even when the job succeeded
The callout fails with 'uncommitted work pending', because the finalizer shares the job's DML
Finalizers can't make callouts, so it must enqueue an `@future(callout=true)` method
It can call out, and `ctx.getException()` holds the error when the result is `UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`
questions.explain: Finalizers are allowed to make **callouts**. They run in a separate transaction, so the job's DML doesn't block them. `getException()` returns the job's error only when `getResult()` is `UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION`; otherwise it's null.
wrong: `getException()` is null when the job succeeds.
The finalizer runs in its own transaction, apart from the job's DML.
Callouts are allowed directly in a finalizer.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: Where does a developer attach a finalizer to a Queueable job?
options: In the code that enqueues the job, by passing the finalizer in `AsyncOptions`
Inside `execute()`, by calling `System.attachFinalizer(new LogFinalizer())`
In a separate class that implements both `Finalizer` and `Schedulable`
In the Queueable's constructor, with `System.attachFinalizer(new LogFinalizer())`
questions.explain: You attach a finalizer **while the job runs**. Call `System.attachFinalizer()` inside the Queueable's `execute()` method. Only one finalizer can be attached to each job.
wrong: `AsyncOptions` sets delay, depth and duplicate checks, not finalizers.
Finalizers attach to Queueable jobs, not scheduled ones.
The constructor runs before the job is queued, not as part of the job.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Finalizers

questions.q: This test of a batch class fails, though the batch works in production. What is the problem?
options: `COUNT()` queries can't be used inside an assertion; assign the count first
`Test.stopTest()` doesn't wait for batch jobs; check the results in a new test method
A test can run only one `execute()`; use 200 or fewer records, or a larger scope
Batch classes can't be started in tests; call `start()`, `execute()` and `finish()` directly
questions.explain: In a test, a batch job can run its `execute()` method only **once**. 300 records at the default scope of 200 need two runs, so the test fails. Use 200 or fewer test records, or a scope big enough for all of them.
wrong: `COUNT()` in an assertion is fine; the record count is the problem.
`Test.stopTest()` does run the batch before the next line.
Tests start batches with `executeBatch` between `startTest` and `stopTest`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex (Best Practices)

questions.q: A batch updates `Inventory__c` stock while warehouse users edit the same records. The developer wants to lock each chunk's records so no edits are overwritten. What should they do?
options: In `execute()`, query the chunk's Ids again with `FOR UPDATE`, then update them
Implement `Database.Stateful`, which locks records between chunks
Set the scope to 1, because one-record chunks are locked automatically
Add `FOR UPDATE` to the `start()` query so every record is locked for the whole job
questions.explain: `FOR UPDATE` in the start query doesn't apply to Batch Apex. Instead, select just the Id in `start()`. Then re-query each chunk with `FOR UPDATE` inside `execute()`. The lock lasts until that chunk's transaction ends.
wrong: `Database.Stateful` keeps variables, not record locks.
Chunk size has nothing to do with locking.
`FOR UPDATE` isn't applicable to a batch's `QueryLocator`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex

questions.q: A team schedules `NightlyPriceSync` with `System.schedule()`. Which two statements about this scheduled class are true? (Choose 2)
options: Member values set before `System.schedule()` are saved with the job; `transient` ones aren't
An org can have up to 250 scheduled Apex jobs at one time
Deploying changes to it fails while jobs are pending, unless Deployment Settings allow it
Its `execute()` method gets a `Database.BatchableContext` that holds the scheduled job's Id
It can call an external API right inside `execute()` if the class also implements `Database.AllowsCallouts`
questions.explain: Scheduled Apex saves the class's state when you schedule it; mark fields `transient` to skip that. You can't deploy a class with pending jobs unless Deployment Settings allow it. Callouts must go through a Queueable or a batch.
wrong: The limit is 100 scheduled Apex jobs at one time.
`execute()` gets a `SchedulableContext`; its `getTriggerId()` returns the `CronTrigger` Id.
Scheduled Apex can't make synchronous callouts; use a Queueable or a batch with `Database.AllowsCallouts`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex Scheduler

questions.q: A nightly batch's `start()` returns `Database.getQueryLocator('SELECT Id, (SELECT Id, Email FROM Contacts) FROM Account')`. It runs much slower than similar jobs. What should the developer change?
options: Raise the scope to 2,000 so that fewer `execute()` calls are needed
Add `Database.Stateful` so the Contacts are cached across chunks
Return an `Iterable` instead, which always processes faster than a `QueryLocator`
Drop the subquery from `start()` and query the Contacts inside `execute()`
questions.explain: A `QueryLocator` with a **relationship subquery** makes the batch use a slower, non-chunking method. Keep `start()` to a plain query. Then fetch the Contacts in `execute()`, one chunk at a time.
wrong: Bigger chunks don't fix the slow mode, and they risk hitting limits.
`Database.Stateful` adds the cost of saving state; it caches nothing.
An `Iterable` also uses the slower, non-chunking method.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex (Best Practices)

questions.q: Batch job B must start only after batch job A has fully finished. What should the developer do?
options: Start both jobs together; the flex queue runs batches strictly one at a time
Call `Database.executeBatch(new BatchB())` in A's `finish()` method
Call `Database.executeBatch(new BatchB())` at the end of A's last `execute()`
Schedule B with `System.schedule()` for one hour after A is started
questions.explain: `finish()` runs once, after every chunk is done. Starting B there **chains** the jobs, so B can't overlap A.
wrong: Up to five batch jobs can run at the same time.
`execute()` can't tell which chunk is last, and chunk order isn't guaranteed.
A fixed delay is a guess; A may take longer than an hour.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex

questions.q: A developer must run `CleanupBatch` once, 60 minutes from now, with a scope of 500. They don't want to write a Schedulable class. Which line does this?
options: `System.schedule('Cleanup once', '0 0 * * * ?', new CleanupBatch(), 500);`
`System.enqueueJob(new CleanupBatch(), 60);`
`System.scheduleBatch(new CleanupBatch(), 'Cleanup once', 60, 500);`
`Database.executeBatch(new CleanupBatch(), 60);`
questions.explain: `System.scheduleBatch()` runs a batch **once**, a set number of minutes from now. It takes the batch, a job name, the minutes and an optional scope. No Schedulable class is needed.
wrong: `System.schedule()` takes a name, a cron string and a Schedulable, with no scope.
`enqueueJob` is for Queueable jobs, and its delay can be at most 10 minutes.
The second number is the scope, so this starts now with chunks of 60.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex (Using the System.scheduleBatch Method)

questions.q: There are 80,000 `Visit__c` records. What happens when this batch starts?
options: It fails at 50,000 rows: an `Iterable` keeps the SOQL row limit
It works, but only the first 2,000 records are passed to `execute()`
It doesn't compile, because `start()` must return a `QueryLocator`
It works, because a batch can always read up to 50 million records, however `start()` is written
questions.explain: Only a `QueryLocator` skips the 50,000-row query limit, up to 50 million records. A list or other `Iterable` still counts the rows, so 80,000 is too many.
wrong: There's no 2,000 cap; the query fails before `execute()` runs.
`start()` may return an `Iterable` or a `QueryLocator`.
The 50 million figure applies only to a `QueryLocator`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex

questions.q: Five minutes after a user submits a loan, the org must re-check the credit bureau once. The team doesn't want to use up scheduled-job slots. Which approach fits best?
options: `System.schedule()` with a cron expression built for five minutes from now
`@future(callout=true, delay=5)` on the method that checks the bureau
`Database.executeBatch(new CreditRecheck(loanId), 5)` with a scope of 5
`System.enqueueJob(new CreditRecheck(loanId), 5)`, a Queueable with a delay in minutes
questions.explain: `System.enqueueJob(job, delay)` starts a Queueable after a **minimum delay** of 0 to 10 minutes. It doesn't take a scheduled-job slot. A cron job would count toward the 100 scheduled Apex jobs.
wrong: It works, but each one uses one of the 100 scheduled Apex job slots.
`@future` has no delay option.
The second argument of `executeBatch` is the scope, not a delay.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Queueable Apex

questions.q: Once a quarter, 2 million `Policy__c` records need a new risk score. Which two statements help the developer pick the right tool? (Choose 2)
options: A future method can take a `QueryLocator` and split the work itself
A batch `QueryLocator` can return up to 50 million records
A Queueable can query all 2 million rows, since async limits are higher
Each batch `execute()` gets a fresh set of governor limits
Batch chunks always run in the order they come from `start()`
questions.explain: Batch Apex is built for big jobs. Its `QueryLocator` can return up to **50 million** records, and each chunk runs as its own transaction with fresh limits. A single Queueable is still capped at 50,000 query rows.
wrong: Future methods take only primitive types, not a `QueryLocator`.
The 50,000-row query limit is the same in sync and async Apex.
Chunks tend to run in order, but the order isn't guaranteed.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using Batch Apex; Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: `Shipment_Ready__e` uses Publish After Commit. What happens when this runs in one transaction with 160 shipments?
options: All 160 events publish, because platform events have no Apex limits
It fails at call 151: each publish counts as one DML statement
Only the first 100 events publish, and the rest wait for the next transaction
It fails after 50 calls, because publishing counts like an async job
questions.explain: For **Publish After Commit** events, each `EventBus.publish()` call counts as one DML statement. The limit is 150 per transaction, so call 151 fails. Build a list and publish it once.
wrong: Publishing uses governor limits like other DML.
Limits throw an error; nothing is held over to another transaction.
Publishing isn't counted against the 50 queued-job limit.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Publish Event Messages with Apex; Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: A platform event trigger creates Cases. The Cases show Automated Process as owner and creator, and large batches of 2,000 events often time out. What should the developer do?
options: Call `setResumeCheckpoint()` before each insert, which makes the next batches smaller
Add `System.runAs()` around the DML in the trigger to switch users
Use `PlatformEventSubscriberConfig` to set a running user and a smaller batch size
Raise the trigger's API version, which makes it run as the user who published
questions.explain: By default, a platform event trigger runs as **Automated Process** with batches of up to 2,000 events. `PlatformEventSubscriberConfig`, set through Tooling or Metadata API, changes both the running user and the batch size.
wrong: A checkpoint marks where to resume; it doesn't set the batch size.
`System.runAs()` only works in test methods.
The API version doesn't change who the trigger runs as.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Configure the User and Batch Size for Your Platform Event Trigger

questions.q: An LWC must show a toast whenever `Order_Shipped__e` is published, using `lightning/empApi`. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: A replay Id of `-2` gets only new events published after subscribing
The component must poll the server every few seconds with `setInterval`
Subscribe to the channel `'/event/Order_Shipped__e'`
Subscribe to the channel `'/data/Order_Shipped__e'`
A replay Id of `-1` gets only new events published after subscribing
questions.explain: Platform event channels use the form `/event/EventName__e`. Replay Id `-1` means 'only new events from now on'. Replay Id `-2` replays all events still kept, then new ones.
wrong: `-2` replays all retained events, not just new ones.
`empApi` pushes events to the page; no polling is needed.
`/data/` channels are for Change Data Capture events.
questions.source: Lightning Web Components Developer Guide: lightning/empApi; Platform Events Developer Guide: Message Durability

questions.q: A trigger on `Payment__e` must send each payment to an accounting API. Callouts aren't allowed directly in the trigger. What should the developer do?
options: Enqueue a Queueable that implements `Database.AllowsCallouts`, passing it the event data
Add `callout=true` to the trigger definition so the trigger itself is allowed to call the API
Throw `EventBus.RetryableException` so the callout runs on the retry
Use `Test.getEventBus().deliver()` to send the events on to the API
questions.explain: Platform event triggers follow trigger rules, so they generally can't make callouts. Hand the work to async Apex. A Queueable with `Database.AllowsCallouts` can make the call.
wrong: Triggers have no `callout=true` option.
A retry runs the same trigger again, still without callouts.
`Test.getEventBus().deliver()` only delivers events in Apex tests.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Subscribe to Platform Event Notifications with Apex Triggers

questions.q: A Pub/Sub API client that processes `Order_Placed__e` events was down for 30 hours. It saved the Replay Id of the last event it handled. What can it do?
options: Query `Order_Placed__e` with SOQL to find the events it missed
Ask an admin to resend the missed events from the Platform Events page in Setup
Nothing: events are deleted as soon as one subscriber receives them
Subscribe again from that Replay Id; events are kept for 72 hours
questions.explain: High-volume platform events are kept for **72 hours**. A subscriber can pass a saved Replay Id to get the events after it. 30 hours is inside that window.
wrong: Platform events can't be queried with SOQL.
Setup can't resend old events; replay them with the Replay Id.
Events stay in the event bus for 72 hours, whoever has read them.
questions.source: Platform Events Developer Guide: Message Durability

questions.q: An ERP listens to `AccountChangeEvent`, then writes its own updates back to Salesforce through the REST API with the client Id `erp-sync`. Each write-back creates another change event, and the loop never ends. What should the ERP subscriber do?
options: Skip any event that has the same `transactionKey` as the one before it
Skip events whose `ChangeEventHeader.changeOrigin` contains `client=erp-sync`
Skip events whose `changedFields` list is empty, since write-backs change nothing
Ask an admin to turn off Change Data Capture for Account while each sync is running
questions.explain: `changeOrigin` names the API and the client Id that made the change. If the ERP sends a client Id when it writes, it can spot and skip its own echoes. That breaks the loop.
wrong: Each write-back is its own transaction, with a new `transactionKey`.
Write-backs do change fields, so `changedFields` isn't empty.
Turning CDC off would miss real user changes during the sync.
questions.source: Change Data Capture Developer Guide: ChangeEventHeader Fields

questions.q: A CDC trigger on `OpportunityChangeEvent` reads `Margin_Pct__c`, a formula field, to decide whether to alert finance. The value is always null, even when the margin changes. Why?
options: The field must first be added to the event's `changedFields` list in Setup
Formula values appear only in the change event that follows this one
CDC doesn't support formula fields, so they're always null in the event
Change event triggers run as Automated Process, which can't see formula fields
questions.explain: Change Data Capture doesn't include **formula fields**. They're null in a change event trigger, changed or not. Query the record, or work the value out from the fields that did change.
wrong: `changedFields` is filled by Salesforce; you can't add fields to it.
No later event carries the formula value either.
Automated Process isn't the reason; CDC never sends formula values.
questions.source: Change Data Capture Developer Guide: Change Event Trigger Considerations

questions.q: A user clears `Fax` and changes `Phone` on an Account. Which two statements about the `AccountChangeEvent` an Apex trigger receives are true? (Choose 2)
options: The trigger runs as the user who edited the Account
`changedFields` is also filled in for record creation events
The trigger runs in the same transaction as the user's save
Fields the user didn't change are null in the Apex event
`nulledFields` in the header lists `Fax`
questions.explain: In Apex, every field exists on the event, but unchanged ones are **null**. That's why `nulledFields` matters: it tells you `Fax` was really cleared. The trigger runs later, as Automated Process.
wrong: Change event triggers run as Automated Process by default.
`changedFields` is empty for create events.
It runs asynchronously, after the change is committed.
questions.source: Change Data Capture Developer Guide: Change Event Triggers; ChangeEventHeader Fields

questions.q: A developer saves an Apex trigger on `Invoice__ChangeEvent` without errors, but it never fires when Invoices change. What is the most likely cause?
options: `Invoice__c` isn't selected on the Change Data Capture page in Setup
Change event triggers must be `before insert`, not `after insert`
The trigger must call `EventBus.subscribe()` once to start listening
Custom objects send change events only for edits made in the UI
questions.explain: You can save a change event trigger for any object. But it only fires once the object is **selected** for change notifications on the Change Data Capture page.
wrong: Change event triggers are always `after insert`.
Triggers subscribe by themselves; there's no subscribe call.
Changes from Apex, the API and the UI all send change events.
questions.source: Change Data Capture Developer Guide: Change Event Trigger Considerations

questions.q: A named credential `Billing_API` points to `https://billing.example.com`. Which line calls `/invoices` with the query string `status=open`?
options: `req.setEndpoint('named:Billing_API/invoices?status=open');`
`req.setEndpoint('https://Billing_API/invoices?status=open');`
`req.setEndpoint('callout:Billing_API').setParam('status', 'open');`
`req.setEndpoint('callout:Billing_API/invoices?status=open');`
questions.explain: A named credential URL starts with **`callout:`**, then the name, then an optional path. You can add a query string after a `?`.
wrong: The scheme is `callout:`, not `named:`.
A plain https URL skips the named credential and its sign-in.
`HttpRequest` has no `setParam` method.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Named Credentials as Callout Endpoints

questions.q: Each sales rep must call a partner's API with their own partner login, so the partner's audit log shows who did what. The endpoint and secrets must stay out of code. What should the developer set up?
options: A hard-coded endpoint, with each rep's password sent in a header
A named credential with an external credential that uses a per-user principal
A named credential with an external credential that uses one named principal for all reps
A Remote Site Setting, plus each rep's token stored in a custom setting
questions.explain: An **external credential** holds the sign-in settings. A per-user principal means each user signs in and gets their own token. Users get access through a permission set mapped to that principal.
wrong: Hard-coded endpoints and passwords are what named credentials avoid.
A named principal makes every rep call as the same partner account.
Custom settings aren't a secure place for tokens, and this puts sign-in logic in code.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Named Credentials and External Credentials; Apex Developer Guide: Named Credentials as Callout Endpoints

questions.q: An LWC calls this method with 4 Ids from the page. What happens?
options: It fails: a timeout of 60 seconds is above the continuation maximum
All 4 callouts run in parallel, and `processChecks` gets 4 responses
It fails: one continuation can hold at most 3 parallel callouts
The first 3 run now, and the 4th runs after `processChecks` returns
questions.explain: A **Continuation** can run up to 3 callouts in parallel, so adding a 4th request fails. Split the work into smaller groups. The timeout can be up to 120 seconds, so 60 is fine.
wrong: Continuation timeouts can go up to 120 seconds.
The cap is 3 parallel callouts per continuation.
There's no automatic queue for extra requests.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Asynchronous Callout Limits

questions.q: This test fails with 'You have uncommitted work pending'. What is the fix?
options: Call `Test.startTest()` before `Test.setMock()`, and `Test.stopTest()` after the call
Use `StaticResourceCalloutMock` instead of `HttpCalloutMock`, because it allows DML before the callout
Add `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)` so the Account no longer needs to be inserted
Call `Test.setMock()` before the `insert`, so the mock is ready earlier
questions.explain: In a test, DML before a mock callout is fine if the callout part sits between **`Test.startTest()`** and `Test.stopTest()`. `startTest()` must come before `setMock()`.
wrong: Every mock type follows the same `startTest()` rule.
Relying on org data makes tests fragile; the right fix is `startTest()`.
The order of `setMock()` and the insert doesn't matter; the DML is still pending.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Performing DML Operations and Mock Callouts

questions.q: In a Lightning controller method, which two operations, run before an HTTP callout in the same transaction, cause 'You have uncommitted work pending'? (Choose 2)
options: An `insert` of a log record
A call to an `@future` method
A `System.debug()` of the request body
Reading a value from a custom metadata type
A SOQL query that reads the Account to send
questions.explain: **Pending work** is something waiting for commit: DML, async Apex such as future or batch jobs, scheduled Apex, or email. Do the callout first. Reads like SOQL or debug lines are fine.
wrong: Debug logging doesn't create pending work.
Reading custom metadata is a query, not pending work.
Queries don't create pending work.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Callout Limits and Limitations

questions.q: A test needs a fake reply from a WSDL2Apex-generated SOAP class. Which line completes this mock?
options: `Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, fake);`
`stub.response_x = fake;`
`return fake;`
`response.put('response_x', fake);`
questions.explain: `doInvoke()` returns nothing. You hand back the fake reply by putting it in the **`response` map** under the key `'response_x'`. The test then calls `Test.setMock(WebServiceMock.class, new QuoteServiceMock())`.
wrong: SOAP stubs use `WebServiceMock`, and `setMock` belongs in the test, not the mock.
`stub` is a plain `Object`; the reply goes in the `response` map.
`doInvoke()` is `void`, so it can't return a value.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Test Web Service Callouts

questions.q: A partner calls an Apex REST class that has no custom status handling. Which two default responses will they see? (Choose 2)
options: 201 whenever an `@HttpPost` method succeeds
400 when the method throws a custom exception that nothing catches
A 302 redirect to the login page when the method throws an unhandled exception
204 when a `@HttpPatch` method with a `void` return succeeds
400 when the URL doesn't match any `urlMapping`
questions.explain: Apex REST sets status codes for you. A custom (user) exception that nothing catches returns **400**; a system exception returns 500. A successful `void` PATCH returns 204, and an unmapped URL returns 404. For anything else, like 201, set `RestContext.response.statusCode` yourself.
wrong: Apex doesn't send 201 by itself; set `statusCode` to 201 in code.
An unhandled exception returns an error code: 400 for a custom (user) exception, 500 for a system exception.
An unmapped URL returns 404.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex REST Methods

questions.q: An `@HttpGet` method returns a `PriceDto` object. The mobile app expects a `discount` key even when it's null, but the key is missing from the JSON. What should the developer do?
options: Mark `discount` as `transient`, so that Apex REST always writes it into the JSON response
Return `void` and write `JSON.serialize(dto)` into `RestContext.response.responseBody`
Change `discount` from `Decimal` to `String`, because String fields are never left out of JSON
Add `@JsonAccess(serializable='always')` to the class so null values are serialized
questions.explain: When Apex REST serializes a return value, it **drops fields that are null**. `JSON.serialize()` keeps nulls by default. So write the JSON yourself into `responseBody` and return `void`.
wrong: `transient` members are left out of serialization entirely.
Null Strings are dropped just like null Decimals.
`@JsonAccess` controls who may serialize the class, not how nulls are handled.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex REST Methods; Apex Reference Guide: JSON Class

questions.q: Class A has `urlMapping='/orders/*'` and class B has `urlMapping='/orders/returns/*'`. A client calls `/services/apexrest/orders/returns/8812`. Which class handles it?
options: Class A, because the shortest pattern is checked first
Class A, because the class that was saved first always wins a clash
Class B, because the longest matching wildcard pattern wins
Neither: overlapping URL mappings make the request fail with HTTP 409
questions.explain: An exact match wins first. If there is none, Salesforce picks the **longest** wildcard pattern that matches. `/orders/returns/*` is longer, so class B handles the call.
wrong: Longer patterns win, not shorter ones.
Save order only settles a tie between `/x` and `/x/*`, which this isn't.
Overlapping mappings are allowed; the longest match wins.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: RestResource Annotation; Apex REST Methods

questions.q: A partner's Java system must call a custom Apex SOAP web service. What does the partner need?
options: The WSDL generated from the Apex class, plus a session Id or OAuth token for each call
The org's Metadata API WSDL, because custom Apex services are defined as part of the metadata
Only the class name, because Apex SOAP services accept anonymous calls
An Apex REST URL, because Apex SOAP services are reached through `/services/apexrest`
questions.explain: Each Apex SOAP class can generate its **own WSDL** from its Setup page. The client builds its calls from it. Every call must be signed in, with a session Id from a login or an OAuth token.
wrong: The Metadata API WSDL is for deploying metadata, not for calling your logic.
Apex SOAP calls need a signed-in session.
`/services/apexrest` is for Apex REST, not SOAP.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Exposing Apex Methods as SOAP Web Services

questions.q: A pricing rule must run from a screen flow and from an LWC on the Quote page. The developer already has an `@InvocableMethod` for the flow. What is the best way to reuse the logic in the LWC?
options: Import the invocable method into the LWC with `@salesforce/apex`, the same way as any Apex method
Make the class `global` so the LWC can call the invocable method directly
Add `@AuraEnabled` to the existing `@InvocableMethod`, so the flow and the LWC share one method
Move the logic into a service class used by both the invocable and an `@AuraEnabled` method
questions.explain: The only annotation allowed alongside `@InvocableMethod` is `@Deprecated`. So keep the real logic in a **service class**. A thin invocable wrapper serves Flow, and a thin `@AuraEnabled` method serves the LWC.
wrong: An LWC can only import Apex methods marked `@AuraEnabled`.
`global` changes package visibility; it doesn't expose a method to LWC.
`@InvocableMethod` can't be combined with `@AuraEnabled`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableMethod Annotation

questions.q: A record-triggered flow on Lead calls an invocable action that checks addresses. When one of 200 Leads in a load has a bad address, the action throws and the whole batch fails. What should the developer change?
options: Throw a custom exception instead, because that fails only the interview that caused it
Catch errors per input and return one result for each, with a success flag and a message
Return results only for the Leads that passed, so the flow quietly skips the bad one
Add `callout=true`, which makes Flow retry the failed interviews one at a time
questions.explain: An invocable method gets all the interviews' inputs in one list. An uncaught exception fails them all. Catch errors per input and **return one result per input**, in the same order, so each interview sees its own outcome.
wrong: Any uncaught exception, custom or not, fails the whole batch.
Outputs must match inputs in size and order, or interviews get the wrong values.
`callout=true` only says the action calls out; it adds no retries.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableMethod Annotation

questions.q: This class is the input type for a flow action. Which two problems must be fixed? (Choose 2)
options: `reason` needs a `label` too, because a `description` on its own isn't allowed
The class must be `global` to be used by a flow in the same org
`currencyCode` can't use `defaultValue` together with `required=true`
`amount` is `private`, but invocable variables must be `public` or `global`
`orderId` can't be an `Id`; flows need record Ids passed as a `String`
questions.explain: Only **`public` or `global`** variables can be invocable variables, so `amount` fails. And `defaultValue` throws an error when used with `required`. `Id` fields and a lone `description` are fine.
wrong: `label` and `description` are both optional.
A `public` class works for flows in the same org.
`Id` is a supported invocable variable type.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableVariable Annotation

questions.q: Admins can't find a new Apex action in Flow Builder because it's listed under Uncategorized. How does the developer list it under 'Billing'?
options: `@InvocableMethod(label='Billing: Create Invoice')`
`@InvocableMethod(label='Create Invoice' iconName='Billing')`
`@InvocableMethod(label='Create Invoice' category='Billing')`
`@InvocableMethod(label='Create Invoice' group='Billing')`
questions.explain: The **`category`** modifier sets the group an action appears under in Flow Builder. Without it, actions show as Uncategorized.
wrong: The label is only the action's name; it doesn't create a category.
`iconName` sets the action's icon, not its category.
There's no `group` modifier on `@InvocableMethod`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: InvocableMethod Annotation

questions.q: A global search box runs this SOSL. Which records does `second` hold?
options: Leads, because the lists follow the order in the `RETURNING` clause
Accounts, because `Account` is a parent object and parents are listed last
Contacts, because the lists are sorted by object name
A mix of all three objects, sorted by search relevance, in one `List<SObject>`
questions.explain: SOSL returns a **list of lists**, one per object. The lists always come back in the same order as the `RETURNING` clause. Contact is index 0, so index 1 is Lead.
wrong: Parent and child links don't change the list order.
SOSL keeps the `RETURNING` order, not alphabetical order.
Each inner list holds just one object type.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Dynamic SOSL; SOQL and SOSL Reference: RETURNING FieldSpec

questions.q: This test always fails, even though the Account is inserted first. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The search index needs time; put `Test.startTest()` and `Test.stopTest()` around the insert
SOSL in tests only sees org data; add `@IsTest(SeeAllData=true)`
Use `Search.query()` instead, because inline SOSL isn't allowed in test methods
Tests return empty SOSL results; set them with `Test.setFixedSearchResults()`
questions.explain: In a test method, every SOSL query returns **empty results** by default. `Test.setFixedSearchResults()` sets the record Ids that later searches return. Any `WHERE` or `LIMIT` in the search still filters them.
wrong: `startTest()` and `stopTest()` don't index records; SOSL stays empty.
Test SOSL is empty by design; the fix is `Test.setFixedSearchResults()`.
Inline SOSL works in tests; it just returns nothing by default.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Adding SOSL Queries to Unit Tests

questions.q: Sales ops wants every Account that has no open Opportunities. Which query returns them?
options: `SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT Id FROM Opportunity WHERE IsClosed = false)`
`SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity WHERE IsClosed = false)`
`SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity WHERE IsClosed = true)`
`SELECT Id, (SELECT Id FROM Opportunities WHERE IsClosed = false) FROM Account WHERE Opportunities = null`
questions.explain: An **anti-join** is `NOT IN` with a subquery. The subquery must return a field that points to the same object, here `AccountId`. So `Id NOT IN (SELECT AccountId … WHERE IsClosed = false)` keeps only Accounts with no open deals.
wrong: The subquery must return `AccountId`, which points to Account, not the Opportunity `Id`.
This semi-join finds Accounts that do have closed deals.
A child relationship can't be compared to null in `WHERE`; use an anti-join.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: Comparison Operators (Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins)

questions.q: A pipeline report groups Opportunities by stage. Which key reads the total Amount from each `AggregateResult`?
options: `'expr1'`
`'SUM(Amount)'`
`'expr0'`
`'Amount'`
questions.explain: Each aggregate without an alias gets an automatic one: `expr0`, `expr1` and so on, counting only the unaliased ones. `MAX(CloseDate)` has the alias `lastClose`, so `SUM(Amount)` is `expr0`.
wrong: `expr1` would be a second aggregate without an alias, and there isn't one.
The function text isn't a key; unaliased aggregates use `expr0`, `expr1` and so on.
`Amount` isn't grouped or aliased, so no key has that name.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Working with SOQL Aggregate Functions

questions.q: A nightly job loops over `[SELECT OwnerId, COUNT(Id) n FROM Task GROUP BY OwnerId]` in a SOQL for loop. The org has about 3,500 task owners. What happens?
options: It fails: aggregate queries can't use `queryMore`, so over 2,000 rows throws
It works, but only the first 2,000 owners are processed, and no error is ever raised
It doesn't compile, because a SOQL for loop can't use `GROUP BY`
It works, because SOQL for loops fetch rows in chunks of 200
questions.explain: SOQL for loops normally fetch rows in chunks with `queryMore`. **Aggregate queries can't use `queryMore`.** So a for loop over an aggregate query that returns more than 2,000 rows throws a run-time exception.
wrong: Going past 2,000 aggregate rows throws; it doesn't stop quietly.
It compiles; the failure happens at run time.
Chunking needs `queryMore`, which aggregate queries don't support.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: SOQL For Loops

questions.q: What happens when this code reaches the last line?
options: Nothing happens, because `sp2` was already used up when the code rolled back to `sp1`
Order C is rolled back, and no Orders are left
Order C is rolled back, and Orders A and B are kept
It fails at run time, because rolling back to `sp1` voided `sp2`
questions.explain: Rolling back to an earlier savepoint also wipes out every **later** savepoint. After `rollback(sp1)`, `sp2` is invalid, and using it throws a run-time error.
wrong: Using an invalid savepoint throws an error; it isn't silently ignored.
The last rollback throws instead of running.
B was undone by `rollback(sp1)`, and `sp2` can't be used at all.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: Which two statements about `Database.setSavepoint()` and `Database.rollback()` are true? (Choose 2)
options: A savepoint saved in a static variable can be used in a later trigger invocation
Static variables keep their values after a rollback
A rollback clears the Ids on sObjects inserted after the savepoint
Each savepoint you set counts toward the DML statement limit
After `rollback()`, the code can make a callout without releasing any savepoint
questions.explain: Savepoints and rollbacks each count as a **DML statement**. A rollback undoes database changes only: static variables and sObject Ids stay as they were. Savepoints can't cross trigger invocations.
wrong: Savepoints can't cross trigger invocations; this throws a run-time error.
Ids stay on the sObjects, which is why inserting them again fails.
Active savepoints must be released with `Database.releaseSavepoint()` before a callout.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: A user deleted several Contacts from the 'Bluefin' Account last week. A developer must restore them in Apex. Which approach works?
options: Call `Database.emptyRecycleBin()` on their Ids, which puts them back
Query them with `WHERE IsDeleted = true ALL ROWS`, then call `undelete` on the list
Query them with `WHERE IsDeleted = true`; deleted rows come back without extra keywords
Query them with `ALL ROWS FOR UPDATE` to lock them, then call `undelete`
questions.explain: Normal queries skip deleted records. **`ALL ROWS`** includes records in the Recycle Bin, so you can find them and `undelete` them. `ALL ROWS` can't be combined with `FOR UPDATE`.
wrong: `emptyRecycleBin()` deletes records for good; it doesn't restore them.
Without `ALL ROWS`, deleted records aren't returned at all.
`ALL ROWS` and `FOR UPDATE` can't be used together.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Querying All Records with a SOQL Statement

questions.q: An import tool reads an object API name, such as `'Shipment__c'`, from Custom Metadata into `objName`. It then sets fields with `rec.put()` and inserts `rec`. Which line creates `rec`?
options: `SObject rec = (SObject) JSON.deserializeUntyped(objName);`
`SObject rec = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(objName).getDescribe().newRecord();`
`SObject rec = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(objName).newSObject();`
`SObject rec = new SObject(objName);`
questions.explain: To build a record whose type is only known at run time, get its **`SObjectType` token** from `Schema.getGlobalDescribe()`. Then call `newSObject()`. After that, `put()` sets fields by name.
wrong: Deserializing a plain name doesn't create an sObject.
There's no `newRecord()` method; `newSObject()` lives on the `SObjectType` token.
You can't create a generic `SObject` with `new`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Understanding Apex Describe Information; Apex Reference Guide: SObjectType Class

questions.q: A lookup helper runs one SOSL search per keyword inside a loop. A user enters 25 keywords. What happens?
options: Search 21 fails: the limit is 20 SOSL queries; use one `FIND` with `OR`
Only the first 20 searches run, and the rest return an empty `List<List<SObject>>`
All 25 run, because SOSL limits apply only inside triggers
All 25 searches run, because SOSL shares the 100 SOQL query limit
questions.explain: A transaction can run only **20 SOSL** queries, sync or async. Search 21 throws a `LimitException`. One SOSL query can search several terms joined with `OR`.
wrong: Search 21 throws; no search quietly returns empty lists.
The SOSL limit applies to every transaction.
SOSL has its own limit of 20, apart from SOQL's 100.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Execution Governors and Limits
